docs.aiSummary: Discusses disposable web design and longevity, listing common symptoms such as poor UX, design fads, broken links and quick fixes, and causes including poor planning, following fads and poor documentation, with advice on building sites that last.

children.text: Longevity takes a different form online, but its value is immeasurable. There is a balance to find. Quick, constant change is given to the web. It is often one of its greatest strengths.

Disposability is a tricky term to handle in the digital world. So many things are changing so quickly — programming languages, frameworks, and design trends, to name but a few — that it often feels inevitable that the things we make will be outdated almost as soon as we finish making them. This is exciting and positive in many ways, but it can also cause long-term thinking to be drowned out by short-term priorities.

This piece is about disposable web design and longevity, with steps to find the sweet spot between reinventing the wheel and twiddling thumbs. Evolution and improvement are promising. We are cutting corners and putting the cart before the horse is not.
Let’s dive into the dos and don’ts of disposable design.
What Is Disposable Design?

Most of us understand what disposable design means in a general sense: good and evil. Disposable design is single-use plastics, which crumbled well before their time. It can be savvy and conscientious, like biodegradable tent pegs at a music festival or scale models. At its worst, it’s short-term thinking and long-term headaches.

In this web design context, we’ll focus mainly on the ‘at its worst’ aspects, with similar nods to times when it can be (and is) very useful. Longevity is a more slippery concept online, but we tend to recognise the sins when we see them. Here is a handful:
Unpleasant UX.

We’ve all stumbled across websites warped out of shape due to a lack of future-proofing. Elements out of place, buttons not working, and the site gently croaking ‘kill me’ are just a few of the things we notice in the seconds before clicking away, never to return.
Following design fads rather than shaping design around content.
Do you remember parallax scrolling? There are good reasons for any feature in the proper context; being cool is not cool. Fads are worse when they clash with the rest.
Broken links, internal and external.
One of the Web’s greatest gifts is links. Dead links rob users of context, destroy the browsing flow, and, perhaps worst of all, waste people’s time.
Ever-growing navigation drawers with no apparent pattern or logic.
Headers are supposed to make navigating the site more accessible, not more complicated.
Quick fixes.
This runs the gauntlet from obvious hotfixes never followed up on to hardcoded snippets with uncanny knacks for breaking everything else on the site.

As well as being frustrating daily, these issues stem from the approach that leaves sites needing replacing or redesigning far sooner than they should. There comes the point where such projects become a resource drain. Sometimes only a new website will do, but every year?
The Causes

In a way, disposable design is the tip of a lousy practice iceberg. There are a lot of potential factors that lead to it, which can wreak havoc elsewhere: some I’ve witnessed (and frankly been guilty of) myself, others from afar.
POOR PLANNING

Fail to prepare, prepare to fail. The maxim rings true in the world of web development. Whether you’re building a portfolio, an e-commerce store, a magazine, a hotel booking site, or whatever else, flimsy planning will lead to unsafe design. If you don’t know what you need, the odds of landing on the correct answer by chance are slim.

Design goes hand in hand with purpose. You wouldn’t build an aeroplane without a blueprint, would you? We need to know the meaning before steaming into making things. I touched on this in What Vitruvius Can Teach Us About Web Design, and there is a near-endless supply of great material on the topic.

As ever, there is a balance to be struck. Things like accessibility, navigation, and information architecture have to be baked into a website early on, while the styling of your hyperlinks can afford to evolve as the site settles. If you set yourself up with a working compass, you don’t necessarily need to know the exact path. You can’t account for everything, but you can undoubtedly point yourself in the right direction and give the project a decent shot at success.
FOLLOWING FADS

The Web evolves much faster than the natural world. Every day brings with it new ideas, new standards, new frameworks, and new possibilities. All that is gold does not glitter, though. There is a fine line between progress and fads, but again we tend to recognise the difference when we see it intuitively.

Parallax scrolling may look snazzy, and that full-page video loop on the home page may have a particular wow factor, but are those things serving the site and its users? Sometimes the answer is yes, and that’s fine, but sometimes they feel overcompensated for lack of substance.
In short, make choices based on what’s suitable for the project, not on what everyone else is doing in a given week.
POOR DOCUMENTATION

Good documentation is so necessary. It forces you to clarify your thinking and give others a fighting chance to understand what you’ve done on earth. Would anyone know how the site works if you fled the country tomorrow? Can the client use it? Are they able to post blog entries themselves and update key content? Usage and handover documentation keep projects alive and growing.

Knowledge hoarding might be good for you, but it’s terrible for the project. Not only does it obscure the inner workings, but it also denies them the outside scrutiny that would likely make them better. Everyone is on the same page about the fundamentals allows you to focus on the more inspiring stuff. (This also is a crucial benefit of using proven frameworks. People may come and go, but at least there’s continuity in the tech, which requires less personalised explanation.)

In fairness, some people have no interest in knowing how certain things work. I don’t like that as an excuse to skip documentation altogether. Anything worth doing is worth doing well for its own sake. Even documentation can be beautiful and inspiring. A friend worked on Stripe integration and linked me to their documentation. I was somewhat floored by how well done it is:
As you scroll through
the documentation
, a preview of the example code highlights the sections you’re reading. We don’t all have to go this far, by why aim for less than excellence?
OUTSOURCING

It’s tempting to embed third-party platforms on websites. It’s easy and spares you the hassle of building something yourself. Why make an image gallery when I can just slap it on my Instagram feed instead? Why maintain a blog when I can just show my Twitter feed? Hell, why build a site at all? Squarespace templates are pretty cool, and it’s not my money anyway.
The answer to most of these questions is that you don’t own content, not on your website. You’re a guest playing by someone else’s rules and usually pay more for the privilege.
A website is the beating heart of your web presence. It won't age well if you outsource your content to third-party platforms.
SHORT-TERMISM

I’ve developed a nervous tick regarding the phrase ‘quick wins.’ This boiled down to short-term thinking and rushed (or nonexistent) preparation. They can be helpful but easily corrupted. Too many quick wins create a disposable design and a race to the bottom. There is no question that time passes faster online, but that doesn’t mean longevity isn’t a worthy goal. If anything, it’s all the more critical.
What, then, does that look like?
Building To Last

In many ways, the ease with which sites can be chopped and changed is one of the web’s greatest strengths. In the real world, junk genuinely impacts the planet — landfills of obsolete tech, abandoned buildings, and beaches piled high with plastics. Not so online. When something is outdated, you press delete and poof! It’s gone. No beaches are piled high with discarded websites; it’s just code. (That said,
the
web's carbon footprint is growing and not to be dismissed.)
What exactly is the benefit of longevity online? And how can it be sustainable given the relentless change we all have to deal with? Jeremy Keith’s presentation
‘The Long Web’

gets to the roots of those questions just as well today as when he delivered it in 2008. For me, it boils down to the direction. If you understand what a site is for, where it’s going, and how it’s likely to change, you can separate what should be constant and what should be flexible.
In some areas, consistency is essential. For example:
URL structure.
Playing fast and loose with page slugs is generally a bad idea. It’s terrible for SEO, dreadful for UX, and a real pain to tidy up.
Branding.

Familiarity breeds… familiarity. Let’s say you run an online store and make wholesale changes to the layout and navigation every few months. Eventually, customers are going to get tired of the constant reinventions.
Content strategy and tone of voice.

What we write and how we write it significantly impact a site’s character. Whether a magazine or a weather forecast web app, unclear, inconsistent writing comes across as amateurish. Conversely, a reliable voice connects the past, present, and future.
Design best practice.

The fundamentals change much more slowly for all the graphic design and UX trends. A site that embraces the basics of typography, colour palettes, grid systems, and navigation is setting itself up to last.
Accessibility.

You can’t retrofit fit website accessibility. Not well, anyway. As Joy Heron writes in her recent piece on ‘Responsible Web Applications,’ failure to do so is frankly irresponsible (and I note that as someone guilty of it myself in the past).

In many ways, disposable design makes change more complicated. It forces you to start from scratch when history tells us it’s generally better to iterate. Sometimes you have to go back to the drawing board — no doubt — but there comes the point where more is to be gained on nailing down a core offering.
SUSTAINABLE WEB DESIGN

Longevity is different online than it is in infrastructure or housing. If a pair of shoes lasts thirty years, what do you have? A good pair of shoes. What do you have if a building stands for centuries and remains structurally sound and helpful? A good building. What do you have if a website is the same as it was thirty years ago? Well,
the Space Jam promo site
. Iconic, but hardly the cutting edge of web design.
The International Space Station has been operating since 1998. It’s almost a quarter of a century old. Modular design and long-term thinking. Hear me out.

Would the total be as cutting edge as a new one from scratch? Not by a long shot, but that is also a testament to its longevity. It’s already the most expensive thing ever built (over $100 billion, baby), so it best makes it last. And yes, one day, there will have to be a successor to the ISS — a rebuild, if you will. They’re already preparing for it.
New modules will be done to detach as part of a separate station.
Neat, huh?

Changeability is part of the design. It is modular rather than a monolith, changing organically over time. For a similar example in the natural world, look no further than your body, which replaces its cells over time. Breaking up projects into different sections or repositories frees you up to innovate without rebuilding the whole thing. Amendments are smoother than rewrites.
RESILIENCE

Making a website’s design last in this way means solving current problems and future issues. Some things are impossible to predict, but others aren’t. Asking the right questions can make a huge difference to longevity. While discussing this topic with Vitaly Friedman, he summarised the process in three simple words: What happens if…?
Some examples of raising your blood pressure a few notches:
What happens if… we have 50 items in the navbar rather than 5?
What happens if… we hit 100 blog posts or 1,000?
What happens if… we have a very dense table with 15 columns on this page?
What happens if… we include a third-party widget that loads 10 external resources?
What happens if… our heaviest page is viewed on the worst possible mobile device with a poor 3G connection?
What happens if… we want to flesh out our
Progressive Web App
functionality?
What happens if… we wish to translate our UI to other languages?
What happens if… the text on a button is lengthy?
What happens if… someone can only navigate the site with a screen reader?
That simple prompt can lead to all sorts of good follow-up questions that you, as a designer, will need to answer. Of all things, I’m reminded of one of
Kurt Vonnegut’s rules for writing fiction
“Be a sadist. No matter how sweet and innocent your leading characters, make awful things happen to them so the reader may see what they are made of.”

Give your websites the same treatment. Subject them to the kinds of (hypothetical) strains and mishaps you wouldn’t wish on your worst enemy. Only then can you see what it is made of and what you must do to make it resilient.

From architecture to manufacturing to space exploration, the value of that inner sadist is immeasurable. Do you think the brains behind the International Space Station haven’t considered every possible way things could go wrong? They probably have a plan for an alien invasion, just in case.
LONGEVITY SUCCESS STORIES
If a space station can function for 20 years without becoming obsolete, websites can too. Indeed, many have. For me, Wikipedia
hit that same benchmark in January
. Despite being one of the most visited, edited sites on the Web, its core offering is now the same as in the early 2000s. If it is not broken…
David Bowie’s Wikipedia page in 2005. (
Large preview
David Bowie’s Wikipedia page in 2021. (
Large preview

At the same time, few would argue the Wikimedia Foundation has been static or behind the times. For example, its Wikidata and Abstract Wiki initiatives serve as nodes, bringing new qualities to the table while enriching the project. Wikipedia and its ‘modules’ endure because they are shaped around a clear purpose and a long-term outlook.
The museum
’s history
is fascinating. Today’s Amazon is wildly different from 1994, but there’s a smooth sense of evolution. It’s hard to look past Amazon.
Baby Amazon, 1997. Source:
eBaum’s World
Large preview
On a less colossal scale, I have nothing but respect and admiration for
Jeffrey Zeldman’s preservation of content from 1995
. (See the ‘Pardon My Archives’ section at the bottom.) A solid 26 years of content. Now there’s a website built to last.

Large preview
Meanwhile, under the hood, examples run across a spectrum. Frameworks like
React
and
Vue
have modular designs baked in via components. With them, a site is not a monolith but a series of bite-sized parts which can be chopped and changed without breaking everything.
Further along the scale, you’ll find the likes of The Guardian,
which publishes its source code on GitHub
. From front-end website code to apps to in-house tools, there are tens of hundreds of repositories and modules that, when pieced together, result in an
award-winning
digital news product. Most of us don’t need thousands of repositories, but the ethos is the same.

There is no one-size-fits-all approach for sustainable web design, but there are recurring principles of purpose, evolution, and long-term thinking. Those qualities allow sites to weather the constant disruptions of the Web.
Sustainability Online

There is nothing wrong with redesigns, migrations, and exploring mysterious new online worlds. There is plenty wrong with doing those things for the wrong reasons, and it will catch up with you eventually. Jeff Huang’s
Manifesto for Preserving Content on the Web
lays out the basics in a way I like very much.
Below are just a few ways to start thinking about the long term:
Don’t just think about next year.
What could it look like in two years or five? Or 20?! What can you do to meet that future gracefully?
Design for accessibility.
Not only is this right for its own sake, but it helps make the content clearer, machine-readable, and better equipped to adapt to evolving technologies.
Think modular.
As is often the case, breaking big projects into smaller pieces makes them more manageable and flexible. Channel your inner International Space Station.

Everyone’s needs are a little different, but the ethos holds. By laying solid foundations, you allow yourself, your peers, and your successors to focus on improvement rather than fixes. It gets us closer to a Web where dead links, by-the-numbers design, and third-party domination are exceptions rather than the norm.

docs.aiSummary: Covers transparency, feedback and ethical AI UX.

children.text: Principles for trustworthy AI experiences.

Adding an AI feature to a product is easy. Getting people to understand it, rely on it and stay in control of it is much harder. Users don't trust a feature because it's clever. They trust it because it behaves predictably, explains itself when it matters and lets them step in when it gets things wrong.
That's the heart of human-centered AI: designing intelligent features around the person using them, not around the model powering them. Here are the principles that make the difference in practice.
Set honest expectations from the start

The first moment someone meets an AI feature shapes everything after it. If your onboarding promises magic, every mistake feels like a betrayal. If it sets clear, modest expectations, people are more forgiving and more likely to keep using it.
Good expectation-setting looks like:
Saying plainly what the feature does and what it doesn't do.
Showing examples of good inputs, so people know how to get useful results.
Labeling AI-generated content clearly, so no one mistakes a suggestion for a fact.
Avoiding human-like personas that imply more understanding than the system has.
Underpromise a little. Users would rather be pleasantly surprised than quietly let down.
Make the system's reasoning visible

People are more comfortable with a decision when they can see roughly why it was made. You don't need to expose model internals. You need to give users enough context to judge whether an output makes sense.
Useful patterns include:
Showing the sources or inputs a result was based on.
Explaining recommendations in a short phrase, such as "because you saved similar items."
Signaling confidence when it varies, so people know when to double-check.
Highlighting what changed when the AI edits something the user created.
Transparency works best when it's light and contextual. A short explanation next to the result beats a long help article nobody reads.
Keep users in control

A human-centered AI feature never traps the user. They should always be able to accept, edit, undo or ignore what the system suggests. Control is what turns an unpredictable feature into a dependable tool.
Design for control by:
Defaulting to suggestions rather than automatic actions for anything consequential.
Making undo fast and obvious.
Letting people adjust or turn off AI behavior in settings they can actually find.
Asking for confirmation before the system acts on someone's behalf in ways that are hard to reverse.
The more impact an action has, the more control the user should keep.
Build feedback into the experience
Feedback loops help in two directions. They let users correct the system in the moment, and they give your team signals about where the feature is falling short.

Keep feedback simple and close to the output. A thumbs up or down, a quick "not relevant" option or an inline edit is far more likely to be used than a separate form. When someone gives feedback, acknowledge it and, where you can, show that it made a difference. Feedback that disappears into a void teaches people to stop giving it.
Design for graceful failure
Every AI feature will be wrong sometimes. The question is how the product behaves when it is. A graceful failure keeps the user moving instead of leaving them stuck or misled.
Plan for the common failure modes:
Low confidence:
say so, and offer alternatives or a manual path.
No result:
explain why in plain language and suggest what to try next.
Wrong result:
make it easy to correct, and don't repeat the same mistake in the same session.
Slow responses:
show progress and let people keep working while they wait.
Write these states with the same care as the happy path. They're often where trust is won or lost.
Respect the user's time and attention

Human-centered AI also means knowing when not to show up. A feature that interrupts constantly, offers suggestions nobody asked for or rewrites work without being invited quickly becomes noise. Let people pull AI help in when they want it, and keep proactive suggestions rare and relevant.
Closing thoughts

Trustworthy AI experiences aren't built on accuracy alone. They're built on honesty about what the system can do, visibility into how it reaches its output, real control for the user and calm, helpful behavior when things go wrong. Design those pieces well and your AI features will feel less like a black box and more like a capable assistant people are glad to work with.

children.text: (Or: How I Lied, Blamed My Junior, Begged Support, and Still Learned Something Useful)
There are two kinds of engineers.
The ones who read the documentation like it’s a sacred text.
And the ones who see a shiny “Get Started” button, mutter “how bad could it be?”, and click it with the confidence of someone who has never been humbled by a free tier.
I am proudly, catastrophically, the second kind.

It started innocently enough. I wasn’t building a production AI product. I wasn’t migrating a client. I was just… curious. I wanted to understand how modern RAG stacks actually fit together — LangChain, vector search, embeddings, the whole circus. I’d been poking around other platforms and coming away mildly disappointed with the developer experience. Then I landed on Netlify’s marketplace and found this:
RAG based chatbot using LangChain and MongoDB Atlas
https://www.netlify.com/integrations/mongodb/rag-based-chatbot-using-langchain-and--atlas-setup-guide/

It looked perfect. LangChain? Check. MongoDB Atlas? Check. RAG? Exactly what I wanted. I already had my own MongoDB Atlas cluster sitting there. My brain filled in the blanks with the optimism of a man who has never read a pricing page carefully: “I’ll just plug in my own database, Netlify will host the frontend, and I’ll be done before lunch.”
Reader, that is not what happened.
What I thought I was deploying was a sample app connected to my own Atlas instance.

What I had actually stepped into was Netlify’s AI ecosystem — AI Gateway, Agent Runners, compute, background jobs, deployments, billing, credits, and a handful of other moving parts that were very clearly documented somewhere I definitely did not read carefully enough.

While I was busy debugging why my MongoDB integration wasn’t behaving the way I expected, credits were quietly evaporating in the background. There were warnings. I ignored them. Not because I enjoy chaos, but because every engineer eventually develops a dangerous little voice that translates free-tier warnings into “That’s probably for people doing real work.”
Lesson one on the road to a Netlify account suspension: credits don’t wait for you to finish reading.
I was apparently doing real work. Then Every Website Went Offline

The next thing I knew, every single project under my Netlify account was offline. Not just the experimental chatbot. Everything. Old client demos. Archived personal sites. Portfolio links. Stuff that had nothing to do with RAG, MongoDB, or my sudden curiosity. Suspended. Account-wide.
That was the moment I learned an important distinction: Netlify doesn’t suspend your experiment. It suspends your
account
So I did what any self-respecting engineer does after confidently breaking production. I wrote an email that was equal parts apology, historical revision, and quiet begging.
“AI credit was enabled mistakenly. I disabled it as soon as I realised. I never intended to use the service… it was an honest mistake by someone.”
Looking back, I may have slightly rewritten history. I even dragged my junior into it.
“…my junior got super excited.”
In fairness, he
was
excited.
Also in fairness, so was I. Curiosity simply outran accountability by a comfortable margin.

To Netlify’s credit — and this genuinely deserves recognition — Joshua replied within hours. Instead of linking me to the pricing page and wishing me luck, he added 200 courtesy credits as a one-time gesture and calmly explained where the credits had actually gone: AI inference, Agent Runners, compute, functions, bandwidth, web requests, production deployments… even verified form submissions. One credit each. Everything had a measurable cost. Not necessarily a large one, but a real one.
I thanked him, disabled everything I could find, congratulated myself on surviving the incident, and moved on.
Fifteen minutes later the account froze again.

That was probably the funniest part in hindsight. Imagine finally convincing support that you’ve fixed everything… and then your account immediately suspends itself like a disappointed parent. I sent another email that basically translated to: “Hi… me again.”

Angelica replied with the missing piece. Even though I had disabled AI, the processes that were already running hadn’t instantly stopped. Background Agent Runs were still finishing, quietly consuming the 200 courtesy credits that had just been added. By the time I checked the dashboard, they were gone. She restored another 300 credits, explained the concept of “ghost” processes still in flight, and somehow managed to do it without making me feel like a complete idiot. (I had already handled that part myself.)

By the next morning I had gone into full damage-control mode. AI features disabled. Netlify Labs disabled. AI usage guardrail set to a dramatic $1. I even emailed support asking whether every GitHub deployment was now secretly costing me money and whether I should just turn off Continuous Deployment entirely.

Michelle clarified it perfectly: only production deployments consume deployment credits. Branch deploys and Deploy Previews remain free. Continuous Deployment itself wasn’t the problem. Continuous Assumption was.
Mary rounded it out by confirming the account was stable again and gently reinforcing how processes already in flight can keep consuming credits even after you’ve flipped the switch.
The Numbers
Looking back, this story isn’t really about MongoDB.
It isn’t about LangChain.
It isn’t even about Netlify.
It’s about assumptions.
I assumed a free tier meant I could experiment in isolation.
I assumed disabling AI would immediately stop everything related to AI.
I assumed the starter template was little more than a frontend wired to MongoDB Atlas.
None of those assumptions were entirely true.

Modern AI platforms aren’t just hosting providers anymore. They’re orchestration layers. Inference, compute, background jobs, deployments, functions, bandwidth, billing — everything is connected, sometimes more tightly than you realise until you’ve already tripped the circuit breaker for the entire account.

So yes. I lied a little. I blamed my junior. I begged. I panicked over emails. I got humbled by a free tier. And I accidentally discovered that one of the fastest ways to understand a platform is to break it just enough that the support team has to explain how it actually works.
To Joshua, Angelica, Mary, and Michelle — thank you.

You could have simply quoted the documentation and closed the ticket. Instead you restored the account twice, answered increasingly embarrassing questions, explained the system with patience, and left me understanding the platform far better than when I started.
That’s good support.
And fortunately for me, it’s a much better story than “I built a chatbot.”

P.S. The MongoDB + LangChain starter itself wasn’t the villain. Neither was RAG. The problem was the quiet confidence of a “Get Started” button and the man who clicked it without reading the fine print. I’ll probably only make that particular mistake once.
(Probably.)

docs.aiSummary: Looks at augmented reality as a UX medium, covering its use in retail try-before-you-buy experiences and utility apps, with Lens Studio and ARKit as starting points, and argues AR should serve real customer journeys.

children.text: Augmented reality is quietly changing UX design. A look at where AR is heading and what it means for immersive product experiences.
This post looks at augmented reality UX: where it already helps people, and what changes when you design for the space around them instead of a flat screen.

Augmented reality has a more immediate application than VR since it only requires a smartphone, letting virtual objects be viewed within the real world. No headset, no special room, no learning curve; just the camera most people already carry in their pocket. That low barrier is exactly why AR is creeping into everyday products faster than VR ever did.
AR in retail

AR lets customers try before they buy, reducing churn and enhancing physical and online shopping alike. Retailers like IKEA and Home Depot already use it to preview furniture and paint in real spaces.

The UX win here is confidence. One of the biggest reasons people hesitate online, or return what they bought, is uncertainty: will this sofa fit, will this shade of blue look right in my living room? Placing a true-to-scale 3D model in your own space answers that question in seconds. The same idea is spreading to eyewear, makeup and sneakers, where virtual try-ons let shoppers experiment without the trip to a store.
AR for utility

Beyond retail, AR apps like measuring tools and location-aware guides have broad utility use cases. Point your phone at a room and get its dimensions. Hold it up on a street and see directions laid over the road in front of you. Scan a machine and see step-by-step repair instructions anchored to the right part.
These experiences work because they put information exactly where it's needed, in context, instead of making people switch between a screen and the world.
What it means for UX designers
Designing for AR means designing for space, not screens. A few things change:
The environment is part of the interface.
Lighting, clutter and room size all affect how an experience feels, so you have to design for messy, unpredictable settings.
Onboarding matters more.
Many users still don't know they need to move their phone around to scan a surface. Clear, gentle guidance makes or breaks the first experience.
Comfort is a constraint.
Nobody wants to hold their arm up for five minutes. Keep sessions short and the payoff quick.
Lens Studio and ARKit are two accessible starting points for building AR experiences.
Designing augmented reality UX that people trust

Good augmented reality UX starts with being honest about what the technology can and can't do. If a virtual sofa hovers slightly above the floor or drifts as the user moves, confidence disappears quickly. A few practices help:
Show scale clearly.
Let people see dimensions, or compare an object against something familiar, so they believe what they're looking at.
Give feedback while tracking.
When the camera is still mapping a surface, say so. A simple hint that the app is "finding the floor" stops people from assuming it's broken.
Make placement forgiving.
Snapping objects to surfaces and allowing easy repositioning saves people from fiddly adjustments.
Offer a way out.
Not everyone can or wants to use the camera at that moment. A standard 2D view should always be one tap away.
Common pitfalls to avoid
Plenty of AR features launch with excitement and are quietly forgotten. The patterns behind that are usually familiar:
AR as a gimmick.
If the experience doesn't answer a real question the user has, it becomes a one-time novelty.
Too much on screen.
Layering labels, buttons and animations over a live camera feed gets cluttered fast. Keep overlays minimal and relevant.
Ignoring accessibility.

Experiences that depend on precise hand movements, sharp eyesight or a well-lit room shut people out. Think about text alternatives, readable contrast against real-world backgrounds and controls that don't need steady hands.
Forgetting privacy.
AR apps see inside people's homes and workplaces. Be clear about what the camera captures and whether anything is stored.
A simple checklist before you build
Before committing to an AR feature, it helps to ask a few practical questions:
What decision or task does AR make easier compared with a photo, a video or a regular screen?
Where will people realistically use it, and what will the lighting and space be like?
How will first-time users learn to scan, place and interact with objects?
What happens on devices that don't support AR?
How will you know it's working? Decide in advance what success looks like, whether that's fewer returns, faster task completion or more confidence before a purchase.

If the answers are vague, a simpler solution may serve users better. If they're clear, prototype early with real people in real spaces, because AR behaves very differently on a tidy desk than in a cluttered living room. Testing in the places where the feature will actually be used is the quickest way to spot problems a desk demo hides.
So, is AR the future of UX?

It's certainly part of it. AR is already useful in the moments where seeing something in context beats reading about it. But AR should stay in service of the customer journeys that matter, not novelty for its own sake.

docs.aiSummary: Introduces actionable UX KPIs.

children.text: Learn which UX metrics influence business outcomes.

Most teams can tell you how a design looks. Far fewer can tell you whether it works. That gap is where good intentions go to die: redesigns ship, opinions get louder, and nobody can say with confidence that the experience actually got better.

UX metrics close that gap. They turn "users seem to like it" into something you can track, compare and defend in a planning meeting. The trick is choosing a small set that reflects real user experience, rather than measuring everything you can and drowning in dashboards.
Start with what "success" means for this product

Before you pick a single number, write down what a good experience looks like for the people using your product. For a banking app, it might be "I can pay a bill quickly and feel sure it went through." For a learning platform, it might be "I can pick up where I left off without hunting."

Those statements become your anchor. Every metric you choose should map back to one of them. If a number doesn't tell you something about those outcomes, it's noise, no matter how easy it is to collect.
Use a framework so you don't miss anything
Google's HEART framework is a useful starting structure because it covers both attitude and behavior. It breaks user experience into five categories:
Happiness:
how users feel, usually captured through surveys or ratings
Engagement:
how much and how often people interact with a feature
Adoption:
how many people start using something new
Retention:
how many keep coming back
Task success:
whether people can complete what they came to do, efficiently and without errors

You don't need all five for every project. Pick the two or three that matter most for the experience you're improving, then pair each with a clear goal, a signal you can observe and a metric you can calculate. Writing out goal, signal and metric side by side keeps the team honest about why a number is on the board.
Task success and time on task
If you only measure one thing, measure task success. It answers the most basic question in UX: can people do what they came here to do?

Define tasks clearly, such as "update a shipping address" or "invite a teammate," and record whether users complete them. Partial completions and wrong-path completions are worth noting separately, because they point to different problems.
Time on task adds depth. A task that gets completed but takes far longer than expected often hides confusion. Just be careful with interpretation:
Compare time on task for the same task across design versions, not across different tasks.
Look at the spread, not only the average. A few very slow sessions can reveal a specific stumbling block.
Remember that longer isn't always worse. On a content page, more time can mean more interest.
The System Usability Scale (SUS)

For a standardized read on perceived usability, the System Usability Scale is hard to beat. It's a short, ten-question survey with alternating positive and negative statements, and it produces a single score you can track over time.

SUS works well because it's quick, it's been widely used for decades, and it's technology-agnostic. Run it after usability tests or at regular intervals with real users. The real value isn't any single score but the trend: is perceived usability rising or falling as you ship changes?
Pair it with one open-ended question, such as "What was the most frustrating part?", so you know why the score moved.
Choosing the right UX metrics
A good metric set is small, stable and actionable. When you're deciding what to keep, run each candidate through a few questions:
Does it reflect a real user outcome, not just activity?
Can the design team influence it directly?
Will it change quickly enough to learn from?
Would a change in this number lead us to do something differently?
Beware of vanity numbers like page views or total clicks. They go up for all sorts of reasons, including bad ones. More clicks can mean people are lost.

It also helps to balance behavioral data (what people do) with attitudinal data (what people say). Behavior shows you where friction lives; attitude tells you how it feels. Together they give you a much clearer picture than either alone.
Connect UX metrics to business outcomes

Experience measures earn their place when stakeholders can see how they relate to results the business already cares about. Higher task success on checkout tends to support conversion. Fewer errors in account setup tends to reduce support requests. Better satisfaction scores tend to support retention.
You don't need to claim precise cause and effect. Show the relationship, track both over time and let the pattern build your case.
Make measurement a habit

Measuring UX success isn't a one-off report. Set a baseline before you redesign, measure again after launch, and keep a simple scorecard that the whole team can see. Revisit your metric set every few months and retire anything nobody acts on.
When you treat these numbers as a way to learn rather than a way to grade, they stop feeling like overhead and start guiding better design decisions.

children.text: Validate before scaling.

Launching a first version feels like crossing a finish line. In reality, it's closer to the starting gun. The minimum viable product gets something real into people's hands, and the real work is figuring out what happens next: do people want it enough to keep coming back, tell others and pay?
That's the journey from MVP to product market fit. It's rarely a straight line, and design plays a bigger role along the way than many teams expect.
What an MVP is

A minimum viable product is the smallest version of a product that lets you learn whether your core idea delivers value to real users. The key word is learn. An MVP is an experiment, not a cheaper version of the final product.
A good MVP:
Focuses on one core problem for a specific group of users
Delivers enough value that people can actually use it
Is built quickly enough that you can change course without regret
Comes with a clear idea of what you want to learn from it
What an MVP isn't
MVPs get misunderstood in a few common ways:
Not a broken product.
"Minimum" doesn't mean unusable. If people can't get value out of it, you can't learn anything from them.
Not a smaller version of everything.
Shipping thin slices of ten features is worse than shipping one feature that works well.
Not the final architecture.
It's fine for parts of it to be manual or temporary. Some MVPs are a landing page, a spreadsheet, or a service delivered by hand.
Not a one-time launch.
You'll likely go through several versions before things click.
What product market fit looks like
Product market fit is the point where a product satisfies a strong demand in a specific market. People don't just try it; they rely on it.
There's no single number that confirms it, but the signals tend to show up together:
Retention flattens.
Some users drop off, but a meaningful group keeps using the product over time instead of slowly fading away.
Usage grows without being pushed.
People come back on their own, not only when you send reminders.
Word of mouth appears.
New users arrive because someone recommended you.
Users would be disappointed without it.
When you ask, a core group says losing the product would genuinely hurt.
Sales get easier.
Conversations shift from convincing to answering questions about details.
If you have to work harder and harder for each new user, and most of them leave soon after, you probably haven't reached fit yet.
The path between the two
Between MVP and fit is a loop of learning and adjusting:
Launch to a focused group.
Pick users who feel the problem most sharply.
Watch behavior, not just opinions.
Track what people actually do: where they activate, where they stall, what they return for.
Talk to the users who stay.
Find out what they value most. That's often the core you should double down on.
Talk to the users who leave.
Understand whether they're the wrong audience or whether something is missing or broken.
Adjust and repeat.
Narrow your audience, sharpen the core value, or rethink the approach entirely if the signals are weak.
Resist the urge to scale marketing or add lots of features during this phase. Growth on top of a leaky product mostly brings in users who leave.
How design helps along the way
Design isn't polish to add after you find fit. It's part of how you find it.
Clarifying the core value.
Design helps decide what the product is really for and strips away anything that distracts from it.
Reducing friction to the first win.
A clear path to the moment users first get value makes it far easier to read whether the value is real.
Prototyping before building.
Testing ideas with prototypes lets you explore directions cheaply between releases.
Running research.
Interviews and usability sessions explain the "why" behind the numbers.
Building trust.
Even an early product needs to feel reliable and credible, or users won't give it a fair chance.
Closing thought

An MVP is a question, and product market fit is a clear answer from the market. Keep your first version focused, measure what people actually do, and let design help you sharpen the core value with each iteration. Scale only once the evidence says people truly want what you've built.

children.text: Product designers are becoming systems thinkers.

Designers entering the field today start in a very different place from those who came before them. They've grown up with design systems, collaborative tools and AI assistants as defaults, not novelties. They often think in components and flows from day one. And they're joining teams that expect more of them, sooner.
How they learn and grow will shape the future of product designers as a whole.
This article looks at the next generation of product designers: what they bring, where they tend to have gaps, and how teams can hire and mentor them well.
What new designers bring
Every generation of designers is shaped by the tools and products they grew up with. Today's newcomers bring real strengths:
Systems-first instincts.
Many learned design through component libraries and tokens, so they naturally think in reusable patterns rather than one-off screens.
Comfort with collaboration tools.
Working in shared files, commenting in real time and handing off to engineers feels normal, not new.
Fluency with AI tools.
They're often quick to use AI for exploration, content drafts and research summaries.
Exposure to many products.
As heavy users of apps and services, they have strong intuitions about what feels modern and usable.
Openness to code.
More newcomers have some frontend experience, or at least aren't intimidated by it.
These strengths make newcomers productive quickly, especially on teams with mature systems.
Where the gaps usually are
The same environment that builds those strengths can leave some gaps. These aren't failings; they're the natural result of how people learn today.
Problem framing.
Tools make it easy to jump straight to solutions. Newcomers may need help slowing down and questioning the brief.
Research depth.
Courses often cover research methods briefly. Running a real study and synthesizing messy findings takes practice.
Working within constraints.
Portfolio projects rarely include legacy code, tight budgets or conflicting stakeholders.
Communicating rationale.
Explaining why a design works, and defending it in a critique, is a skill that develops with experience.
Judging AI output.
Using AI is easy. Knowing when its output is generic, wrong or off-brand takes a trained eye.
How to hire them well
Hiring for potential is different from hiring for experience. A few approaches help:
Look for thinking, not polish.
A rough project with clear reasoning tells you more than a polished one with no story.
Use realistic exercises.
Short, scoped challenges with real constraints show how candidates handle ambiguity.
Ask about decisions.
"Why did you choose this approach?" and "What would you change?" reveal more than "Walk me through your process."
Value curiosity.
Candidates who ask good questions about your product and users often grow fastest.
Be clear about support.
Tell candidates how mentoring works on your team. The good ones will ask.
How to mentor them
Mentoring a new product designer is one of the highest-leverage things a senior designer can do. Some practices that work:
Pair on real work.
Let newcomers shadow research sessions, design reviews and stakeholder meetings before leading them.
Give context, not just tasks.
Explain the business goal and the user problem behind each assignment.
Critique the reasoning.
Focus feedback on decisions and trade-offs, not only on visual details.
Create safe space for questions.
Regular one-on-ones signal that not knowing is normal.
Gradually increase ownership.
Start with a well-defined feature, then a small project, then a problem with open scope.
Teach the system's why.
Newcomers may use components fluently without knowing why they exist. Explaining the reasoning builds better system contributors.
What teams gain

Investing in new designers isn't charity. Teams that do it well get fresh perspectives on their products, people who challenge outdated habits, and a pipeline of designers who understand the team's systems deeply.
There's also a benefit for senior designers. Mentoring forces you to articulate principles you may have stopped questioning. That reflection often improves your own work.
Building the next generation together

The next generation of product designers arrives with strong systems instincts and modern tool fluency. What they need from teams is context, real constraints and thoughtful feedback on their reasoning. Hire for curiosity and thinking, mentor with intention, and give them room to grow into ownership.
If you lead or work alongside new designers, pick one practice from this list and try it this month. Small changes in how you mentor can shape a whole career.

children.text: The Big Idea:
How a human-centered approach helped us transform ParcelShop’s app, making sending and receiving packages feel incredibly easy and intuitive for everyone.
This ParcelShop UX case study walks through the problem, the research and the key screens we designed.
The Problem: When Good Intentions Meet Hard Realities

You know those traditional courier shops? The ones just for sending packages? Well, they’re facing a tough time. Rent, especially in prime spots, is just too high to make them profitable like they used to be. But what if we could flip that script?

Imagine your local bakery, that friendly grocery store, or even your neighborhood laundromat, becoming a spot where you can drop off a package. This isn’t just about cutting costs; it’s about making life easier for everyone and breathing new life into local businesses.
My Role & The Tools We Used
My Hat as UX/UI Designer:
I got to dive into user research, figure out the best ways for people to interact with the app, make it look good, build prototypes, test them out, and sort out how all the information would flow.
Our Go-To Tools:
Sketch, InVision, Photoshop, and Illustrator.
Why This Matters Now: Unpacking the Opportunity

Think about it: a local parcel drop-off point is super convenient. They’re usually close by (90% of customers within 3km!), have longer hours, and offer that personal touch. And with rents skyrocketing in places like Mumbai and New Delhi (we’re talking Rs 5 lakh a month for a shop in Khan Market!), courier companies have to find smarter ways to operate.
This whole idea is a win-win-win:
For Courier Companies (like BlueDart):
It tackles those tricky logistics and keeps costs down.
For Local Businesses:
Hello, extra income! Plus, it brings new faces into their shops.
For Us, the Customers:
Unbeatable convenience for all our parcel needs.
Our Mission: Bringing Courier Bookings to Your Fingertips
The Task:
We needed to design a mobile app that lets small businesses — a bakery, a grocery, a laundromat — easily take courier bookings for a company like BlueDart India.
What We Delivered (and Why It’s Great):
Extra Cash for Shops:
A brand-new way for local retailers to earn.
Smoother Sailing for BlueDart:
Operations get simpler, no complex headaches.
No Clunky Computers:
Forget expensive desktop setups; it all happens on a phone.
How We Got There: Our Iterative Design Journey
We took an iterative approach, meaning we kept refining and improving the design based on what we learned. Think of it as building something, testing it, learning, and then making it even better.
Just a heads-up: For this case study, we’re focusing on the core stuff that really makes a difference.

body.alt: My approach: exercised in five parts
body.caption: My approach: exercised in five parts

children.text: Phase 1: Research — What Users Really Needed
During our research, tons of interesting ideas popped up. But we kept our eyes on the prize: what did shopkeepers and customers really need to make this work?
Shopkeepers told us:
They needed a simple dashboard for pickups and earnings. Speed and fewer steps were crucial.
Customers told us:
They wanted instant price quotes and clear, easy tracking.
Phase 2: Wireframing — Sketching Out the Basics
Once we knew what people needed, we quickly sketched out wireframes. This is like drawing a rough blueprint, just to get the basic layout and flow right before adding all the fancy details.
Phase 3: Design — Making It Look Good and Work Great
Now, let’s jump into the actual app screens. I’ll walk you through some key parts and explain why we designed them the way we did.
1. The Home Screen: All You Need at a Glance
We wanted this screen to be super useful for the shopkeeper right away, but also flexible enough for future additions.
Top Priority:
“Pending Pickups” is right there at the top. This is the most urgent thing a shopkeeper needs to know.
Motivation Boost:
We put “Earnings” front and center. Seeing that money helps keep people motivated!
Ready for More:
The dashboard area is designed to grow, ready for more stats and info as we learn what’s most valuable.
Always Handy:
The sticky footer with “Home,” “Quote,” “Create,” and “Track” means key functions are always just a tap away.
2. Instant Quotes: No Surprises, Just Prices
Our research showed that most customers check prices first. So, we made a dedicated “Quote” page that’s quick and clear.
Simple & Fast:
Just punch in the package size, weight, where it’s going, and how fast, and boom — you get a price estimate.
What’s Next:
In a real-world product, we’d add service types (like “Ground” or “Air”) because those really affect the price.
3. Creating a Shipment: Smooth Sailing, Step-by-Step
We designed the “Create Shipment” process like a friendly wizard, breaking it down into easy steps. No overwhelming screens full of forms!
Smart Saving:
Ever fill out a form only to realize you did this for the same person last week? Our app spots that and asks if you want to use previous data. Super handy, and it cuts down on repetitive typing.
Peace of Mind:
Once payment’s confirmed, both the sender and receiver instantly get a receipt and a tracking ID link. No guessing, just clear communication.
Extra Option:
If the customer needs packaging materials, the shop can easily add that to the booking.
4. Tracking: Knowing Where Things Stand
For pickups at a static shop, we focused on the key milestones.
Clear Stages:
We kept it simple: “Scheduled,” “Delivered,” and “Returned.” No need for complex movement tracking when the package is just sitting there waiting.
(Future thought):
Full, dynamic tracking with an AWB number would be a cool feature to add later, but for this version, simplicity was key.
Looking Ahead: What’s Next on Our Horizon
I’m actually pretty excited about some future possibilities, especially using cool tech to make things even smoother.
Augmented Reality (AR) for Parcel Sizing:

Imagine just pointing your phone camera at a package, and the app instantly tells you its size! This isn’t science fiction anymore. It could save so much time, reduce errors, and make measuring super easy. I’d love to explore this in a real product.
Wrapping Up: Just the Beginning
This case study is a quick look at the core design ideas for ParcelShop. If I had more time, I’d dive deeper into:
Onboarding:
Making it super easy for new shopkeepers to get started.
Multiple Partners:
How the app could work with other courier companies.
Payment Options:
Adding even more ways to pay.
More Research:
Always more to learn from users to make it even better.
Ultimately, this isn’t just about building an app; it’s about making local businesses the heart of convenient parcel delivery.

children.text: Effective product discovery reduces risk.

Building software is expensive. Building the wrong software is more expensive, because you pay for it twice: once to make it, and again to maintain or remove it. Product discovery is the work you do before committing to build, so you can find out early whether an idea is worth the investment.
Done well, discovery doesn't slow teams down. It saves them from long detours. Here's a practical way to run it.
What product discovery is for
Discovery helps you answer four questions before you write production code:
Value:
Will people want this, and will they choose to use it?
Usability:
Can they figure out how to use it?
Feasibility:
Can we build it with the time, skills and technology we have?
Viability:
Does it work for the business, legally, financially and operationally?
Most failed features failed on one of these. Discovery is about testing the riskiest of them as cheaply as possible.
Start with the problem, not the idea
Ideas are easy to fall for. Before exploring solutions, get clear on the problem:
Who is experiencing it?
When and how often does it happen?
What do they do about it today?
What does it cost them in time, money or frustration?

Talk to real users. A handful of focused conversations will usually tell you more than a long internal debate. Look at support tickets, sales notes and product analytics for patterns. Write the problem down in one or two plain sentences so the whole team can agree on it.
List your assumptions
Every idea rests on things you believe but haven't proven. Make them visible. A simple exercise:
Write the idea at the top of a page.
List everything that must be true for it to succeed. For example: "Users want to share reports with their managers," or "Managers will open a shared link."
Rate each assumption by how important it is and how much evidence you have.
Focus first on assumptions that are both critical and weakly supported.
This step keeps discovery honest. Instead of trying to validate the whole idea at once, you test the parts most likely to break it.
Run small, fast experiments
Once you know your riskiest assumptions, design the smallest test that could prove them wrong. Some common options:
Interviews:
good for understanding needs, motivations and current behavior.
Clickable prototypes:
useful for testing whether people understand a concept and can complete key tasks.
Fake door tests:
a button or link for a feature that doesn't exist yet, to measure interest before building.
Concierge or manual tests:
deliver the service by hand to a few users to see if the value is real.
Technical spikes:
short investigations by engineers to check whether something is feasible.
Before each experiment, decide what result would change your mind. Without that, it's easy to read any outcome as a success.
Decide what to build
Discovery should end in a decision, not a slide deck. After your experiments, sort ideas into three groups:
Build:
the key assumptions held up, and you have a clear path forward.
Rethink:
some assumptions failed, but the problem is still worth solving. Go back and explore other solutions.
Drop:
the problem isn't significant enough, or the idea fails on value or viability.
Dropping an idea is a good outcome. It means discovery did its job and saved you from building something nobody needed.
Make discovery continuous
Discovery works best as an ongoing habit, not a phase that happens once before a big project. A few ways to keep it running:
Talk to users every week, even briefly.
Have designers, product managers and engineers take part in research together, so insights don't get lost in handoffs.
Keep a shared space for assumptions, experiments and findings.
Run discovery for the next set of work while delivery continues on the current one.
When product discovery runs alongside delivery, the team always has validated work ready to pick up.
Common mistakes to avoid
Treating discovery as a way to confirm decisions already made.
Asking users what features they want instead of learning about their problems.
Running experiments that are too big or too slow to learn from.
Keeping engineers out of discovery until the design is finished.
Closing thought

Good product discovery is less about methods and more about humility. You assume you might be wrong, and you look for the cheapest way to find out. Keep your experiments small, your decisions clear, and your conversations with users frequent. The work you choose to build will be stronger for it.

children.text: Measure impact, not just visuals.
This is a practical guide to product metrics for designers: what to track, why it matters and how to use it.

Designers are usually great at explaining why a screen looks the way it does. It gets harder when someone asks what that screen did for the product. Did more people get started? Did they stick around? Did they pay?

Those questions are about product metrics, and they're increasingly part of a designer's job. You don't need to become an analyst. You just need to know which numbers describe the health of the product, how your work moves them, and how to use them to make better calls.
Why product metrics belong in design conversations
Usability tells you whether people can use something. Metrics like activation and retention tell you whether the product is working as a business: whether people find value, return and stay.

When you understand these numbers, a few things change. Your design decisions get easier to defend. You can spot problems before they show up in a quarterly review. And you earn a seat in conversations about priorities, not just execution.
Activation: the first moment of value

Activation measures how many new users reach a meaningful first outcome. That outcome is different for every product. For a project tool, it might be creating a first project and inviting a teammate. For a photo editor, it might be exporting a first edit.
Designers have enormous influence here, because activation lives in onboarding, empty states and first-run experiences. To work with it:
Agree with your team on what the activation event actually is.
Map every step between sign-up and that event.
Remove, defer or simplify anything that doesn't help someone get there.
If activation is weak, more marketing won't fix it. Better design often will.
Retention: are people coming back?
Retention measures how many users keep using the product over time. It's one of the clearest signals that you've built something people genuinely need.

Retention is usually viewed in cohorts: groups of users who started in the same week or month, tracked over time. If newer cohorts retain better than older ones, your product changes are probably helping.
Design levers for retention include reminders that respect the user, saved progress, habits built around a regular task, and features that grow more useful as people put more into them.
Engagement: depth, not just frequency
Engagement looks at how people use the product once they're in. Common measures include how often users return in a given period, which features they use, and how many core actions they complete.

The key is choosing engagement measures tied to value. Time spent in an app isn't automatically good. For a tax tool, less time might mean a better experience. Ask: "What does a user who's getting real value actually do?" Then measure that.
Conversion: turning intent into action
Conversion measures how many people complete a step you care about, such as moving from trial to paid, from free to upgraded, or from cart to purchase.

Conversion is where small design details show up most visibly. Pricing clarity, form length, trust signals and the wording on a button all play a part. Break conversion into a funnel so you can see exactly which step loses people, then focus your design effort there rather than redesigning the whole flow.
Churn: understanding why people leave

Churn is the flip side of retention: the share of users or customers who stop using or paying for the product in a given period. It's often the most painful metric to look at, and one of the most useful.

Designers can help in two ways. First, by fixing the friction that pushes people out, which usually means revisiting onboarding, core workflows and billing experiences. Second, by designing a respectful exit flow that asks why someone is leaving. Those answers are some of the most honest feedback you'll get.
How designers can put product metrics to work
You don't need access to every dashboard to use these numbers well. Start with a simple routine:
Pick one metric per project.
Tie each design initiative to the number it should move.
Get a baseline.
Ask your product or data partner for current numbers before you ship.
Write a hypothesis.
"Simplifying the setup screen will improve activation" is something you can test.
Check results after launch.
Look again once there's enough data, and share what you learned, good or bad.
Pair numbers with qualitative insight.
Metrics show what changed. Interviews and session reviews explain why.
Be careful not to chase one number at the expense of everything else. A pushy upgrade prompt might lift conversion and quietly increase churn. Watch related metrics together.
Design for outcomes

Product metrics don't replace craft. They give it direction. When you know what activation, retention, engagement, conversion and churn look like for your product, every design decision has a clearer purpose.
Start small, stay curious and keep connecting your work to outcomes. Over time, you'll find that measuring impact makes you a better designer, not just a more persuasive one.

children.text: Designers benefit from roadmap visibility.
Here's a practical guide to the product roadmap for designers: what it is, the common types, and how to read and influence one.

A roadmap can feel like something that happens to designers rather than with them. Priorities get set in a planning meeting, dates appear on a slide, and the design team inherits a queue. But a product roadmap is one of the most useful documents in any company if you know how to read it, and one of the easiest to influence if you know where to push.
Understanding roadmaps helps you see what's coming, why it matters, and where your work fits into the bigger picture.
What a product roadmap is (and isn't)
A product roadmap is a plan that communicates where a product is heading and roughly when. It connects strategy to the work teams will do.
It is not:
A promise with fixed dates for every item
A complete backlog of tasks
A specification of how each feature should look or behave
Good roadmaps are about direction and priorities. The details get worked out by the teams doing the work, including design.
Common types of roadmaps
Not every roadmap looks the same. Recognizing the type helps you understand what it's really telling you.
Timeline roadmaps
show features or projects laid out against dates or quarters. They're common, easy to read, and often over-trusted. Treat later items as intentions, not commitments.
Now, Next, Later roadmaps
group work by priority rather than dates. "Now" is in progress, "Next" is coming soon, and "Later" is a set of ideas still being shaped. This format is honest about uncertainty.
Outcome-based roadmaps
organize work around goals, such as improving onboarding completion or reducing churn, rather than specific features. They leave room for teams to decide how to reach each goal.
Theme-based roadmaps
group work into broad areas of investment, like performance, collaboration or mobile. They're useful for showing balance across the product.
Many companies use a mix, with a high-level roadmap for leadership and a more detailed one for teams.
How to read a roadmap as a designer
When you look at a roadmap, read past the feature names. Ask:
What goals sit behind these items?
If they aren't stated, find out. The goal shapes the design far more than the feature label does.
Where are the dependencies?
Items that rely on each other may need shared patterns or components planned early.
What's the confidence level?
Something marked for next month might already be well defined. Something marked "Later" is probably still open.
What's missing?
Notice user problems you know about that aren't represented. That's useful input for the next planning cycle.
Where does research need to happen?
Big bets further out are perfect candidates for early discovery.
Reading this way turns the roadmap from a to-do list into a map of opportunities.
How designers can influence the roadmap
You don't need to own the roadmap to shape it. Designers bring evidence that product managers and leaders often lack.
Bring user insight early.
Share research findings before planning starts, not after the roadmap is set. Short, clear summaries of user pain points go a long way.
Frame ideas as problems and outcomes.
Instead of pitching a feature, describe the problem, who it affects and what improvement you'd expect.
Flag hidden effort.
Some items look small but need new patterns, content or research. Raising this early helps planning stay realistic.
Propose design investments.
Work like design system updates or usability fixes rarely gets requested. Make the case by linking it to speed, quality or user outcomes.
Partner with your product manager.
The strongest influence comes from planning together rather than reacting to decisions afterward.
When the roadmap changes

Roadmaps change, and that's healthy. New information, shifting priorities or market changes should affect the plan. As a designer, keep your work flexible where uncertainty is high. Explore lightly for "Later" items and save the detailed work for things that are truly next.
Closing thought

A product roadmap tells you where the product is heading, but it's only as good as the thinking behind it. Learn to read it critically, ask about the goals behind each item, and bring your user insight into planning early. When you do, the roadmap stops being something handed to you and becomes something you help write.

children.text: Why successful teams prioritize outcomes over features.

Shipping feels like progress. A new button goes live, a release note goes out, a ticket moves to done. But a busy roadmap isn't the same as a better product. Plenty of teams ship every sprint and still can't say whether their users are better off.
That gap is what product thinking vs feature thinking comes down to. One measures how much you build. The other measures what changes because you built it.
What feature thinking looks like
Feature thinking starts with a solution. Someone asks for a dashboard, an export option or a dark mode, and the request becomes a ticket. Success means delivering it on time.
You can spot it by a few signs:
Roadmaps are lists of features with dates attached.
Requests come in already shaped as solutions.
Teams celebrate launches, then rarely look back.
Nobody can explain which metric a feature was meant to move.

Teams stuck here are often called a "feature factory." Work flows in, work flows out, and the product grows wider without getting better. Over time, it also gets harder to use, because every addition adds weight.
What product thinking looks like
Product thinking starts with a problem and an outcome. Instead of "build an export button," the question becomes, "Why do people need to get their data out, and what happens if they can't?"

Maybe the real need is sharing a report with a manager. An export might solve that. So might a shareable link, a scheduled email, or a simpler summary view. Product thinking keeps those options open long enough to choose the right one.
It rests on a few habits:
Define the problem before discussing solutions.
Tie every piece of work to an outcome you can observe.
Measure after launch, and be willing to change course.
Say no to good ideas that don't serve the current goal.
Outcomes vs output
Output
is what the team produces: features, screens, releases.
Outcomes
are the changes in behavior that output is meant to cause: more people completing onboarding, fewer support tickets, more teams inviting a colleague.
Output is easy to count, which is why it takes over. Outcomes are harder to measure and slower to show up, but they're the only thing that tells you whether the work mattered.
A helpful test: if you shipped this and nothing in user behavior changed, would you call it a success? If the honest answer is no, you're aiming at an outcome. Make that outcome explicit.
How to frame work around problems and metrics
Changing how work is framed is the most practical way to shift a team's thinking. Try rewriting incoming requests in this shape:
Problem:
What is the user struggling with, and how do we know?
Who:
Which users does this affect, and how often?
Outcome:
What behavior would change if we solved it?
Metric:
How will we see that change?
Options:
What are two or three different ways we could solve it?

This takes a few extra minutes per request, but it changes the conversation. Stakeholders start describing pains instead of prescribing features. Designers and engineers get room to propose better solutions.
Escaping the feature factory
You rarely get to flip a whole organization at once. Start where you have influence.
Ask "why" early.
When a request arrives, ask what problem it solves before estimating it.
Add a success line to every ticket.
One sentence describing the expected outcome is enough to start.
Review results, not just releases.
Set a date a few weeks after launch to check whether the metric moved.
Retire what doesn't work.
Removing a feature that didn't help is a real win, even if it feels like going backward.
Share what you learn.
When an outcome-led change works, tell the story. It makes the case better than any argument.
Product thinking is a team habit

Product thinking isn't a role or a title. Designers practice it when they question the brief. Engineers practice it when they suggest a simpler path to the same result. Product managers practice it when they protect focus. The more people on the team think this way, the less the roadmap looks like a checklist.
Closing thought
Features are tools, not goals. Keep asking what problem you're solving and how you'll know it's solved. Do that consistently, and the product starts getting better instead of just getting bigger.

children.text: Understanding psychology creates better experiences.

Every product is used by a human brain, with all its shortcuts, limits, and habits. When a design works with those tendencies, it feels intuitive. When it works against them, people feel confused or tired without quite knowing why.

Product psychology is the practice of applying what we know about how people think and decide to the way products are designed. Used well, psychology in product design makes products easier and more satisfying. Used carelessly, it slides into manipulation. This article covers a handful of well-known principles and how to apply them responsibly.
Hick's law: fewer choices, faster decisions
Hick's law describes a simple idea: the more options people have, the longer it takes them to decide. Every extra choice adds a little mental effort.
How to apply it:
Limit the number of options on key screens, especially for primary actions
Break long lists into clear categories
Highlight a recommended option when most people would benefit from it
Hide advanced settings until they're needed
This doesn't mean you should always offer fewer things overall. It means structuring choices so people aren't facing all of them at once.
Fitts's law: make important targets easy to hit
Fitts's law states that the time it takes to reach a target depends on its size and distance. Big, nearby targets are fast to hit. Small, distant ones are slow and error-prone.
In practice:
Make primary buttons large enough to tap comfortably, especially on mobile
Place frequent actions where hands and cursors naturally are
Keep related controls close together
Put destructive actions, like delete, away from common ones to avoid accidental taps
It's a simple principle, but it explains why so many small, crowded buttons feel frustrating.
Cognitive load: respect limited attention
Cognitive load is the amount of mental effort a task requires. People have limited working memory, so every extra thing to remember, compare, or interpret makes a task harder.
Ways to reduce it:
Show, don't make people remember.
Keep important information visible instead of on a previous screen.
Chunk information
into small, scannable groups.
Use familiar patterns
so people don't have to learn new ones.
Remove anything nonessential
from the moment of a decision.
Lower cognitive load is one of the most reliable ways to make a product feel easy.
Social proof: people look to others
When people are unsure, they often look at what others are doing. Reviews, ratings, testimonials, and usage indicators all draw on this tendency, which is known as social proof.
Use it honestly:
Show genuine reviews, including mixed ones, rather than only glowing quotes
Display real activity, not inflated numbers
Place social proof where people are making a decision, such as near pricing or sign-up
Fake reviews and made-up counters may work briefly, but once people notice, the damage to trust is hard to undo.
Habit loops: build value people return to

Many products people use daily follow a simple loop: a cue prompts an action, the action brings a reward, and over time the behavior becomes routine. Understanding this loop helps you design products that fit naturally into people's lives.
To build healthy habits:
Tie your product to a real, recurring need people already have
Make the core action quick and easy to repeat
Ensure the reward is genuine value, like progress made or a task completed
Let people control notifications, so cues help instead of nag
The key test is whether the habit serves the user. A habit that helps people reach their goals is good design. One that keeps them scrolling against their own interest is not.
Using product psychology ethically

Every principle above can be bent toward manipulation. Hick's law can be used to bury the cancel option. Social proof can be faked. Habit loops can become compulsive. That's why ethics has to be part of how you apply product psychology, not an afterthought.
A few guardrails help:
Align with user goals.
Ask whether the person would thank you if they understood what you were doing.
Be transparent.
Don't hide information people need to make a good decision.
Preserve choice.
Make it as easy to say no, leave, or undo as it is to say yes.
Avoid exploiting vulnerabilities,
such as fear, urgency, or loneliness, to drive metrics.
When in doubt, choose the option that you'd be comfortable explaining to your users directly.
Final thoughts

Understanding how people think is one of the most useful tools in product design. Hick's law, Fitts's law, cognitive load, social proof, and habit loops can all make your product clearer and more satisfying. Apply them with respect for the people using your product, and psychology becomes a way to help rather than persuade.
