children.text: Great products continuously learn from users.

Many teams treat research like a phase. You run interviews at the start, test a prototype in the middle, then ship and move on to the next thing. The problem is that users don't stop changing when you launch. Their needs shift, their context changes, competitors raise expectations, and the product itself grows in ways nobody fully predicted.
That's why continuous user research matters more than any single study.

Continuous discovery is the practice of staying in regular contact with the people you design for, long after the first release. It isn't a bigger research project. It's a smaller, steadier habit that keeps decisions grounded in what's actually happening.
Launch is where the real learning starts

Before launch, you're working with assumptions and prototypes. After launch, you have real people using a real product in real situations. That's the richest source of insight you'll ever have, and it's a shame to ignore it.

Live usage reveals things no test can: workarounds people invent, features they never find, edge cases you didn't design for, and needs that only appear after weeks of use. Teams that stop researching at launch miss all of it, then wonder why the roadmap feels disconnected from customers.
What continuous discovery looks like in practice
The core idea is simple: small, frequent touchpoints with users, run by the people making product decisions. Rather than a big study every six months, you might:
Talk to at least one or two users every week.
Run a quick test on a new idea before it goes into a sprint.
Review support conversations and feedback on a regular schedule.
Check product analytics for unexpected patterns, then follow up with real conversations.
The cadence matters more than the volume. A steady rhythm keeps the team close to users and makes research feel normal rather than special.
Make it a team habit, not a specialist task

This approach works best when designers, product managers and engineers all take part. When the people building the product hear users directly, they make better small decisions every day, without needing a report to tell them what to do.
A few ways to share the load:
Rotate who leads the weekly conversation, and invite others to listen in.
Keep a shared interview guide so anyone can run a session confidently.
Hold a short debrief right after each call while details are fresh.
Post one key takeaway in a shared channel so the wider team stays informed.
If you have dedicated researchers, their role shifts toward coaching, improving methods and handling the bigger, deeper studies.
Keep recruiting simple
The biggest barrier to ongoing research is usually finding people to talk to. Solve it once and the habit becomes much easier to keep.

Build a lightweight pipeline: an in-product prompt inviting users to share feedback, an opt-in list of customers happy to be contacted, or a standing arrangement with your support or sales team to flag interesting accounts. Automate scheduling where you can, so booking a call takes minutes, not days.
Connect what you learn to what you build
Research only matters if it changes decisions. Continuous discovery should feed directly into how you choose and shape work.

One helpful approach is to map opportunities, meaning user needs, pain points and desires, against the outcomes you're trying to achieve. When a new idea comes up, ask which opportunity it addresses and what evidence you have. Then test the riskiest assumption behind it before committing a full build.
This keeps the team focused on solving real problems rather than shipping features because someone asked loudly.
Watch for the warning signs
It's easy for a discovery habit to fade. Look out for these signs:
Weeks pass without anyone on the team talking to a user.
Roadmap items are justified by opinion rather than evidence.
The same complaints keep appearing in support but never reach planning.
Research findings live in documents nobody revisits.
When you notice them, don't launch a big initiative to fix it. Just book a few conversations this week and restart the rhythm.
Research is never finished
Products are never really done, so research can't be either. Every release creates new questions, and every user conversation reveals something you didn't know to ask.

Continuous discovery isn't about doing more research. It's about doing a little research all the time, so learning becomes part of how your team works. Keep the cadence small, keep it shared and keep it connected to decisions. That's how great products keep getting better long after launch.

children.text: Best practices for designing ethical AI systems.

AI systems make decisions that affect real people: what they see, what they're offered, how they're assessed and sometimes what they're denied. When those decisions go wrong, the harm isn't abstract. It lands on someone who usually had no say in how the system was built.

Responsible AI design is the practice of building these systems so they're fair, respectful of privacy and accountable for their outcomes. It isn't a compliance checkbox at the end of a project. It's a set of questions you ask from the first sketch onward. Here are the principles worth building into your process.
Start with the question of harm
Before asking whether an AI feature is useful, ask who it could hurt. Many ethical problems are visible early if you look for them deliberately.
Run a simple harm review at the start of any AI project:
Who is affected by this system's output, including people who never use the product directly?
What happens if it's wrong for a particular person or group?
Could it be misused, and by whom?
Is AI actually the right tool here, or would a simpler, more predictable approach work better?
Sometimes the most responsible decision is not to automate a judgment at all.
Design for fairness and against bias
AI systems learn from data, and data reflects the world it came from, including its unfairness. A model trained on skewed or incomplete data can quietly treat some groups worse than others.
Designers can't fix bias alone, but you can make it harder to ignore:
Ask who is underrepresented in the data and the research.
Test with a diverse range of people, not just the most convenient participants.
Check outcomes across different groups, not just overall performance.
Avoid inputs that act as proxies for sensitive traits, such as zip code standing in for ethnicity or income.
Treat fairness as an ongoing check, because systems drift as data changes.
Treat privacy as a design material
AI features often want more data, and the temptation is to collect everything just in case. Responsible AI flips that instinct. Collect what you need, explain why, and protect it carefully.
Practical privacy habits include:
Minimizing data collection to what the feature genuinely requires.
Being clear about whether user data is used to train models.
Offering meaningful settings to limit or delete stored data.
Avoiding inferences people would find intrusive, even when the data technically allows them.
If a user would be surprised to learn how their data is used, that's a strong sign the design needs rethinking.
Make consent real
Consent buried in a long terms-of-service page isn't really consent. People should understand what they're agreeing to and have a genuine choice.

Good consent design is specific, timely and reversible. Ask at the moment it's relevant, explain the consequence in plain language and make it as easy to withdraw as it was to give. Avoid dark patterns such as pre-ticked boxes or confusing double negatives. They may lift opt-in rates, but they erode trust and invite regulatory attention.
Build in accountability
When an AI system makes a decision, someone needs to own it. Accountability means people can understand what happened, challenge it and get it put right.
Design accountability into the product and the organization:
Provide a clear way for users to question or appeal significant decisions.
Keep a human in the loop for high-stakes outcomes such as access to money, health or employment.
Log decisions so they can be reviewed and explained later.
Name an owner for each AI system who is responsible for monitoring its behavior.
Keep reviewing after launch

Ethical issues don't stop at release. Usage patterns change, data shifts and new risks appear. Schedule regular reviews of how the system is performing, listen closely to complaints and edge cases, and be willing to pause or roll back a feature if it's causing harm.
Make it easy for your own team to raise concerns too. People closest to the work often spot problems first, and they need to feel safe saying so.
Closing thoughts

Responsible AI isn't about slowing innovation down. It's about building systems people can trust because they were designed with care for everyone they touch. Ask about harm early, design against bias, treat privacy and consent seriously and make sure someone is always accountable. Those habits protect your users, and over time they protect your product too.

children.text: Having a data-driven foundation is profoundly important when making informed business decisions. But what restaurant manager in their right mind would spend time and money extensively tracking data and performing analytics when they have to constantly be on top of managing their staff, ordering supplies, maintaining customer satisfaction, and keeping track of the thousands of other tiny details necessary to run a successful restaurant?
Is that being said, especially when managers need more technical and financial training, it can be tough to answer this deceptively complex, ever-important question: How is my business doing?
But what if analysis could be easy?
(it can be)

In this article, I will discuss how I utilise my experiences, observations and research to empathise and synthesise action points, which I then used to ideate an innovative restaurant insights dashboard.
This is my approach to restaurant sales dashboard design, from the problem through to the components.
Introduction

To understand how this will work, I am taking the example of Biryani Blues. They offer the best biryani and an array of traditional Nizami dishes. From Andhra Chicken Fry, Chicken/Paneer 65 to the Mutton Shikhampur for starters and Dalcha, Salan and Kormas for mains, every word consists of the wealthiest spices to lend the most authentic flavour possible.
They have 25+ outlets across Delhi/NCR
Their USP is reasonable quantities of quality biryani at a mid to high price range
They are operating on multiple online channels — UberEats, Swiggy & Zomato
Problem
Critical challenges in operating a restaurant:
Managing daily, weekly and monthly sales targets to reach business profitability goals.
An overview of your business — both from a day-to-day perspective and a bird's eye view
Gives insights based on available data

Numerous complex interactions and relationships are intertwined amongst each source, and there are often many more sources than those listed. This allows for in-depth exploration, so someone should be analysing this.

Restaurants often perform numerical analyses on these data sources to track their key metrics. These analyses can be instrumental when performing standard calculations, such as keeping up with overall sales trends and seeing the essential cost of goods sold margins. But:
Numbers alone are narrow (and dull)
Trying to gain insights from raw statistical numbers alone only helps show part of the story. It can become a very time-consuming and challenging process once business questions become more complex:
What concrete benefits are we seeing from running our specials/promotions?
What times of day can we adjust staffing based on traffic?
Why are we always missing so many onion?
The benefits of visual analytics across any industry are honest, tangible, and well-documented (a great breakdown of the advantages of visualising data can be found here).

Another problem that is a blocker to more sales that I have witnessed over the years (as someone who orders food delivery multiple times a week) is the difficulty restaurants face maintaining in-house delivery personnel. Personnel heads out for delivery, new orders arrive just moments after s/he has left, and the customer experiences long wait times. The dispatch planning could be more ad-hoc, resulting in inefficiencies. The dispatch planning could be more ad-hoc, resulting in inefficiencies.
How will they compare the data with many outlets and campaigns on different channels: cashback, discounts, and or points?

Restaurants typically want to maintain their delivery fleet (outside delivery services by mobile app-based companies) to cater to orders they receive directly from customers via various channels (phone, website, social media, messaging apps, etc.).
Mobile app-based delivery services charge restaurant owners a commission which eats into a significant portion of their profit margins.
Image: The Financial Express
Possible Solution

To sell more, restaurants need insights into consumer habits and demands. In the past, restaurants tried to develop new and relevant offers and promotions that perfectly fit consumer tastes. We would make educated guesses, and whenever the request met consumers' demands, it would significantly increase sales — for example, lunch discounts on certain days of the week to draw in the office/corporate crowd.
To make sense of this immensely segregated consumer data, a dashboard would help reign in on a restaurant's service delivery optimisation.

For instance, many restaurants now actively hire people with job descriptions that demand them to be able to manage multiple food delivery apps to fulfil orders and operate at scale. A unified dashboard would make the lives of these individuals easier and be critical to the restaurant's success.
Also:
“Elaborate usability tests are a waste of resources. The best results come from testing no more than 5 users and running as many small tests as you can afford.”
Source:
https://www.nngroup.com/articles/why-you-only-need-to-test-with-5-users/
User Persona

Following are the user personas of a restaurant manager, James, and Kevin, the Owner/Marketing head of the entire Biryani Blues — which accurately depicts the typical end-users of our dashboard design.

children.text: Research & Ideation

Having clearly defined the goals, I sketched using pencil and paper. I remembered that most restaurants typically use some form of point of sale (mainly focused on billing and inventory management rather than providing detailed, contextual and actionable insights). Therefore, I am designing an improvement or an additional feature to their existing system.
User Selection Type

Since there are two users, we need to have two views for the panel, one for the outlet view and the other as the admin view covering the entire 25+ outlets. Also, an option to select outlet, channel type and date is added to give detailed insight.

The common theme among these solutions is that they all provide order and sales trend data. However, they need a clear sense of what this data aims to solve, making it less user-friendly to interpret. For instance, simply telling me about popular orders and sales trends does not tell me what needs improvement.

To further help the end user, we need to provide more controls to the data so that it can be easily manipulated and filtered to extract contextual meaning. Examples of other variables we can bring into the dashboard are the time of order and the number of charges for each menu item at a granular level, making this all filterable and easily digestible.

Customer analytics isn’t just for online commerce anymore. The product is to measure KPIs of the brand’s valuable physical stores just as the brand would with your online store and Improve Store Conversion Ratio with the power of Artificial Intelligence. It helps the brand accurately understand store delivery patterns to optimize staffing, store performance and the conversion ratio
Components of Dashboard
We are discussing the elements in a detailed view w.r.t. to channels/outlets and any existing campaign/loyalty/voucher.
1. New User
This will inform us about the overall new users and the channels from where they are coming. On selecting the section of the pie chart, the selected area will update the value.
2. Active Customers
This will update us about the active customers-overall, and most from any channel and most active outlet
3. Customer Overview
Customer served:
The number of unique customers who have shopped for the selected period will populate.
One-timer Customer:
The number of customers whose order count is one and who have ordered for the selected period will populate here.
Repeat customer:
The number of repeat customers will populate here for the selected period.
4. Sales
This section will display sales for the selected period for the store
Overall:
It is the sum of the sales
Campaign:
The sum of bills has a mobile Number mapped to them.
Percentage:
It is Campaign as the percentage of overall sales.
5. Bills
For the selected period,
Overall:
This section will display the count of bills.
Campaign:
The count of bills has a mobile Number mapped to them.
Percentage:
It is Campaign as a percentage for overall bills.
6. ABV — Average Bill Value
is the Average bill value for the selected period,
Overall:
This section will display the average of all bills.
Campaign:
Sum of all sales which has mobile Number mapped to it divided by the count of unique bills
7. UPT — Unit Per Transaction
It is a Unit per transaction for the selected period; this section will display the quantity of the SKU item per unique bill Id.
Overall:
It is the sum of the sales divided by the total number of bills
Campaign:
It is the sum of all sales which has mobile Number mapped to it divided by the total of the bills
8. Discount
For the selected period,
Overall Discount:
This section will display the sum of the total Dvalue.
Campaigns:
Are the sum of the campaign discount. It will have the customer details of GV/Coupon and Points.
9. Campaign Contribution
Number of bills:
All bills with loyalty discount greater than zero
Sales:
It will have the below sections
Absolute Number: Sum of bills with loyalty discount column greater than zero
Percentage: Is the percentage of the sum of all bills
10. Score/NPS — Net Promoter Score
Net Promoter Score, basis shared data, the score will populate.
11. Customer Percentage
Active:
Total Number of customers with the percentage of energetic customers.
Lapsed:
Total Number of customers with the percentage of lapsed
Product Performance Overview
The graph representation shows sales for the products for a given period.
The x-axis shows the top/bottom ten products, and the y-axis shows sales.
The secondary axis shows the Unit of items sold.
The pie chart will show the top overall categories.
Campaign Overview
On hovering following things will be displayed for all three channels:
Count of bills
Sales amount
ABV
UPT
No. of Items
Discount
Cards in the Campaign Overview
Campaign Discount:
Total Amount given as Discount on Coupon redemption for the selected period for the given store. This detail will come from the coupon offer report.
Campaign Sales:
Sum of bills where coupons were redeemed.
Coupons Redeemed:
Total Number of points redeemed.
Coupons Redemption Sales:
Sum of bills where points were redeemed.
Further Testing & Improvements

So many elements can be added, from Detailed Business Reviews to Product performances, Monthly Retention Cohorts, and Active Campaigns lists. Also, clicking on the data trends and getting grouped data on customer demographics such as age, gender, location and so on — to segment the restaurant customers better and deliver the service experience to their unique preferences.
Product UI

Conclusion

Being able to visually see the data from all facets of your business operations at once with a custom-built dashboard makes it incredibly easy to find the answers to almost any business question. There is excellent ROI — you may even be able to find out that Jeff has been stealing cucumbers this whole time. Invest in one, and welcome your restaurant to the modern age of analytics.

children.text: Frameworks for enterprise UX maturity.

Growing a design team inside a large organization is a different job from doing great design work. You can have talented designers and researchers and still end up with a fragmented product, duplicated effort and teams that don't learn from each other. Enterprise UX succeeds or fails on structure: how teams are organized, how work flows between them, and how consistency holds up when dozens of squads are shipping at once.
This guide covers the main team models, the operational backbone that supports them, and the practices that keep quality consistent at scale.
Choosing a team structure
There are three common ways to organize UX in a large company. None is universally right. Each suits a different stage and culture.
Centralized
All designers and researchers sit in one team, led by a single UX leader, and are assigned to projects as needed.
Strengths:
consistent standards, strong craft community, easier career paths, a clear voice in leadership.
Weaknesses:
can feel like an agency to product teams, designers may lack deep product context, and prioritization becomes a bottleneck.
Embedded
Designers and researchers are placed directly in product teams and report to product or engineering leads.
Strengths:
deep product knowledge, close collaboration with engineers, fast decisions.
Weaknesses:
designers can become isolated, standards drift between teams, and craft growth depends on local managers who may not be designers.
Hybrid
Designers work day to day inside product teams but report to a central UX organization. Sometimes called a "centralized partnership" model.
Strengths:
product context plus shared standards and community, with career growth managed by design leaders.
Weaknesses:
dual reporting lines need clear agreements, or people end up serving two masters.

Many large organizations end up with a hybrid model because it balances the benefits of the other two. Whatever you choose, be explicit about who sets priorities, who reviews work and who handles career development.
Building the operational backbone

As teams grow, the hidden work multiplies: tooling, onboarding, research logistics, licenses, hiring pipelines. Without support, designers spend more time on admin than on design. This is where design operations comes in.
DesignOps typically covers:
Tools and workflows.
Standard design tools, file structures and handoff processes.
Research operations.
Participant recruiting, consent, incentives and a shared repository of findings.
People and process.
Onboarding, career frameworks, rituals like critiques, and resourcing across teams.
Measurement.
Tracking team health, project throughput and the impact of UX work.
You don't need a large ops team to start. Even one person focused on operations can free up significant designer time and make the whole team more consistent.
Keeping consistency at scale
When many teams build in parallel, consistency won't happen by accident. A few mechanisms do most of the work:
A shared design system.
Common components, tokens and guidelines give teams a default way to build. Treat it as a product with its own owners and roadmap.
Design principles.
A short set of principles helps teams make similar choices even when they're solving different problems.
Cross-team critique.
Regular reviews where designers from different products look at each other's work spread good ideas and catch drift early.
Pattern governance.
Clear rules for when a team can introduce a new pattern and how it gets shared back.
Shared research.
A searchable repository stops teams from repeating studies and helps insights travel.
Working with the rest of the enterprise

Enterprise UX doesn't operate in a vacuum. Legal, compliance, security, brand and IT all shape what gets shipped. Build relationships with these groups early. Invite them into reviews, understand their constraints and look for ways to make compliance part of the design process rather than a final gate. That turns potential blockers into partners.

Leadership alignment matters just as much. Connect UX work to goals executives already care about, whether that's customer satisfaction, operational efficiency or digital adoption, and report progress in their language.
Growing without losing quality
Scaling fast can dilute quality. A few practices help protect it:
Hire for a mix of seniority so experienced designers can mentor newer ones.
Define clear role expectations at each level so quality standards are shared.
Protect time for craft, such as critique and exploration, not just delivery.
Invest in onboarding so new hires learn the system, principles and tools quickly.
Common pitfalls
Growing headcount faster than the ops and leadership to support it.
Letting each business unit build its own design language.
Treating the design system as a side project.
Measuring UX by output, like screens delivered, instead of outcomes.
Structure that serves the work

There's no perfect org chart for enterprise UX. The right structure is the one that gives designers product context, keeps standards shared and lets the team grow without fragmenting. Choose a model deliberately, support it with operations, and invest in the systems and rituals that keep everyone building the same product.

children.text: Design systems help startups move faster.

That can sound backwards. Startups are supposed to be scrappy, shipping quickly and fixing things later, and a design system sounds like something big companies build with dedicated teams. But the right kind of system, sized for where you are, is one of the cheapest ways to keep speed from turning into mess.

The trick with design systems for startups is to treat them as lean tools, not showcases. You don't need a documentation site with fifty components. You need just enough shared structure that every new screen doesn't start from zero.
Signs it's time to start
You don't need a system on day one. If you have one designer, one engineer and a handful of screens, consistency mostly lives in your heads. The need shows up as you grow. Watch for these signals:
You have more than one person designing or building UI.
The same element, like a button, form field or modal, has been built several different ways.
Engineers ask "which gray is this?" or eyeball spacing from screenshots.
Small visual changes, like updating your brand color, require edits in many places.
New hires take a while to figure out how things are "supposed" to look.
If two or three of these sound familiar, you're already paying the cost of not having a system. You're just paying it in time instead of planning.
The minimum viable system
Start with the foundations that touch everything, then add components only when you need them. A practical first version looks like this:
Color tokens.
A small palette with semantic names: primary action, text, muted text, border, surface, success, warning, error.
Type scale.
Four to six text styles covering headings, body and small text. Fewer is better.
Spacing scale.
A consistent set of steps, for example multiples of four or eight, used for padding, gaps and margins.
A handful of core components.
Button, text input, select, checkbox, card and modal cover a surprising amount of product UI.
One page of rules.
A short shared note explaining naming, when to add something new, and who to ask.
That's it. Put the tokens in code as variables, mirror them in your design tool with the same names, and you have a working startup design system.
Build from real screens, not imagined ones

The fastest way to over-engineer is to design components for situations you don't have yet. Instead, let the product lead. When you build a new feature, look at what you just made. If a pattern appears in two or three places, pull it into the system. If it only appears once, leave it where it is.
This keeps the system honest. Every component in it has earned its place by being used, and you avoid maintaining pieces nobody touches.
Avoiding over-engineering
Startups change direction often, and a heavy system makes change harder. A few habits keep yours light:
Skip edge-case variants until they're needed.
A button with three sizes and two styles is enough for most products early on.
Prefer an existing component library as a base.
Many open source libraries give you accessible, tested building blocks. Theme them with your tokens rather than building every component yourself.
Don't build a docs site yet.
A shared page and well-named components in your design file and codebase are enough until the team grows.
Allow exceptions, but log them.
If a screen needs something custom, ship it and note it. Revisit the list occasionally to see what should become part of the system.
The goal isn't perfection. It's removing repeated decisions so the team can focus on the product.
Who owns it

Early on, ownership can be part time. Usually one designer and one engineer share responsibility: they review additions, keep design and code names aligned, and clean up drift. Give it a small, regular slot, such as an hour every couple of weeks, rather than waiting for a big cleanup that never happens.
As you add designers and engineers, that slot naturally grows. At some point it may become a dedicated role, but you don't need to plan for that now.
What you get back
A small system pays off quickly in ways you'll feel day to day:
New features ship faster because the basic pieces already exist.
The product looks and feels coherent, which builds trust with early customers.
Rebrands and theme changes become an afternoon of token updates instead of weeks of hunting.
New team members get productive sooner because the rules are written down.
Start small, keep it alive

Every startup design system should start smaller than feels comfortable. Tokens, a type and spacing scale, a few core components and a short page of rules will carry you further than you expect. Grow it only when real product needs ask for it, and keep someone looking after it. That's how a system helps you move faster instead of slowing you down.

children.text: Learn the technology stack that supports digital products.

Every product you design sits on top of layers you rarely see. When a button doesn't behave the way you expected, or a "small" change turns into a two-week estimate, the reason usually lives somewhere in those layers. You don't need to master them. You need a map.

This guide walks through the technology stack behind most modern digital products, layer by layer, with just enough detail to help you collaborate well with the people who build it. Treat it as a primer on the tech stack for product designers, not a course in engineering.
What a stack is

A technology stack is the combination of tools, languages and services a team uses to build and run a product. Think of it as a building: the interface is the part people walk through, but it rests on plumbing, wiring and a foundation.
Most stacks break down into five layers:
Frontend
: what users see and interact with.
Backend
: the logic that runs on servers.
Database
: where information is stored.
CMS
: where content is managed by non-developers.
Hosting and infrastructure
: where everything lives and how it reaches users.
APIs connect these layers, carrying data between them.
Frontend: where your designs become real

The frontend is the code that runs in the user's browser or on their device. On the web, it's built with HTML for structure, CSS for styling and JavaScript for behavior. Most teams use a framework like React, Vue or Svelte to organize that code into reusable components.
Why it matters to you:
Components map to your design system.
If your designs are built from consistent components, engineers can reuse code instead of rebuilding similar pieces.
Responsive behavior is code.
Breakpoints, layout shifts and touch targets are all frontend decisions.
Native apps are different.
iOS and Android apps use their own languages and platform conventions, which affects what's easy and what isn't.
Backend: the logic you don't see

The backend handles everything that shouldn't or can't happen on the user's device: checking passwords, processing payments, applying business rules, sending emails. It's written in languages like Node.js, Python, Ruby, Go or Java.

When a design depends on a rule, such as "show this offer only to customers who signed up in the last month," that rule usually lives in the backend. Changing it may be more work than changing a screen, which is why it helps to raise these rules early.
Databases: how information is shaped
Databases store the product's data: users, orders, messages, settings. There are two broad families:
Relational databases
(like PostgreSQL or MySQL) store data in tables with defined relationships.
Document databases
(like MongoDB) store flexible records that can vary in shape.

The structure of the data shapes what the interface can do. If your design shows a user's activity grouped by project, but the database doesn't connect activity to projects, that's a data change, not a design tweak. Asking "how is this stored?" can save a lot of back-and-forth.
CMS: content without code

A content management system lets editors and marketers update content without a developer. Traditional platforms like WordPress handle both content and presentation. Headless CMS tools like Sanity, Contentful or Strapi store content and deliver it through APIs to any frontend.
For designers, the CMS matters because:
Content models define flexibility.
If a page is built from structured blocks, editors can rearrange sections. If it's a fixed template, they can't.
Real content breaks layouts.
Editors will write longer headlines and upload odd-sized images. Design for the range, not the ideal.
Hosting and infrastructure: how it reaches people

Hosting is where the code runs. Many teams use cloud providers like AWS, Google Cloud or Azure, or platforms like Vercel and Netlify that simplify deployment. A content delivery network (CDN) stores copies of files closer to users so pages load faster.
This layer affects performance, reliability and cost. It's also why image sizes, video choices and heavy animations are design decisions with technical consequences.
The goal is shared understanding
You don't need to choose frameworks or configure servers. Use your map to have better conversations:
When you start a project, ask which stack it uses and sketch the layers on one page.
When a design touches data, ask where that data lives and how it's structured.
When something is estimated as "large," ask which layer the work sits in.
When content is involved, look at the CMS before designing templates.

Knowing the technology stack doesn't change your role. It changes the quality of your collaboration. You'll design within real constraints, spot expensive ideas before they're committed, and earn trust with engineers because you speak a little of their language.
Pick one product you work on and learn its stack this month. A short conversation with a developer is often all it takes.

children.text: Marketing is undergoing one of the most significant organizational shifts since the rise of digital.
Welcome to the era of the AI-native marketing team.

For decades, marketing teams have been structured around channels, campaigns, and functional expertise—brand managers, media planners, CRM specialists, creative teams, analysts, and performance marketers. While these roles remain important, Artificial Intelligence is fundamentally changing how marketing operates.
As AI takes over repetitive execution and increasingly autonomous decision-making, marketers will spend less time managing processes and more time designing systems.
The future of marketing will not be built around managing campaigns.
It will be built around orchestrating intelligent agents.
From Functional Teams to AI-Native Organizations
The next generation of marketing organizations will be powered by five foundational AI capabilities:
Continuous Insights
Scaled Creativity
Hyperpersonalization
Marketing to AI Agents
Always-on Orchestration
These capabilities are transforming marketing from a sequence of disconnected activities into an intelligent, continuously learning operating system.
As a result, entirely new roles are beginning to emerge—roles focused not on execution, but on governance, orchestration, trust, and strategic decision-making.
1. Agent Whisperer

As AI assistants and autonomous agents become increasingly involved in product discovery, evaluation, and purchasing decisions, brands must learn to communicate with machines as effectively as they communicate with people.
The Agent Whisperer is responsible for ensuring that AI systems accurately understand, interpret, and recommend the brand.
This role develops machine-readable content, structured knowledge, metadata, and governance frameworks that improve discoverability, credibility, and trust across AI ecosystems.
Rather than optimizing only for search engines, the Agent Whisperer optimizes for intelligent agents.
Their success will be measured not only by customer engagement but also by how effectively AI systems can retrieve, interpret, and recommend the brand.
2. Full-funnel Navigator
Traditional marketing leaders often manage individual functions—brand, demand generation, media, CRM, or analytics.
The Full-funnel Navigator takes a fundamentally different approach.
This role oversees the entire customer journey as an interconnected system.

Working alongside AI agents, the Full-funnel Navigator continuously monitors performance, adjusts priorities, optimizes investments, and ensures every marketing function contributes toward common business objectives.
Instead of managing campaigns, they orchestrate an adaptive ecosystem where insights, creativity, personalization, and automation operate in harmony.
Their responsibility is not execution.
It is coordination.
3. Hyperpersonalization Architect
Personalization has historically relied on customer segments, predefined rules, and limited behavioral triggers.
AI enables something far more sophisticated.
The Hyperpersonalization Architect designs the intelligence behind one-to-one customer experiences.
This role develops the data models, AI decision frameworks, customer profiles, and governance systems that determine how every interaction is personalized.
Equally important, the role establishes ethical guardrails, regulatory compliance, privacy standards, and quality controls to ensure personalization remains accurate, transparent, and trusted.
In an AI-native organization, personalization becomes an operating capability rather than a marketing tactic.
4. Customer Wayfinder
Data has never been scarce.
Meaning has.
The Customer Wayfinder bridges this gap by combining AI-generated intelligence with human judgment.
Rather than simply reporting customer behavior, this role interprets it.

Using customer data, synthetic audiences, cultural signals, qualitative research, and AI-generated hypotheses, the Customer Wayfinder identifies emerging needs, validates ideas, anticipates market shifts, and helps shape strategic direction.
Their role is to ensure that organizations do not merely react to customers—they stay ahead of them.
The Marketer of the Future
These emerging roles do not replace marketers.
They elevate them.
As AI assumes responsibility for execution, optimization, and repetitive decision-making, human expertise shifts toward strategy, governance, creativity, ethics, and systems thinking.
The marketers who thrive in this environment will be those who understand how to guide intelligent systems rather than compete with them.
Success will depend less on operating marketing tools and more on designing the intelligence that powers them.
Looking Ahead
Every major technological shift has reshaped organizational structures.
The internet created digital marketing teams.
Social media created community managers.
Mobile transformed customer experience functions.
Artificial Intelligence is now creating an entirely new category of marketing professionals.
Organizations that begin building these capabilities today will be better positioned to adapt as AI becomes the foundation of modern marketing.
The future of marketing belongs not simply to organizations that adopt AI—but to those that redesign their teams, processes, and operating models around it.

children.text: Artificial Intelligence is no longer an emerging technology. It has become a strategic priority.
Nowhere is this more visible than with AI in marketing strategy.

Organisations across industries are investing heavily in generative AI, agentic systems, and intelligent automation. Budgets continue to grow, pilots are multiplying, and executives increasingly view AI as essential to long-term competitiveness.
Yet despite this momentum, a paradox has emerged.
While AI adoption is accelerating, sustained improvements in business performance remain elusive.

This dynamic closely resembles the Solow Paradox, in which technological advancement becomes widespread, yet measurable gains in productivity and economic value take far longer to materialise than expected.
The problem isn’t a lack of AI.
It’s a misunderstanding of where AI creates value.
Productivity Is Not a Competitive Strategy
Most organisations have approached AI as a productivity tool.
They automate workflows, reduce manual effort, summarise meetings, generate content faster, and streamline internal operations. These initiatives undoubtedly improve efficiency.
However, productivity gains alone rarely create a lasting competitive advantage.

History shows that operational efficiencies are quickly replicated. Competitors adopt similar technologies, markets adapt, and benefits are eventually passed to customers through lower costs, improved service, or faster delivery.
The result is higher efficiency — but not necessarily higher profits.
Organisations that view AI purely through the lens of productivity risk optimising yesterday’s business model rather than creating tomorrow’s.
AI Is Changing the Economics of Competition
The real opportunity lies elsewhere.
AI has the potential to reshape products, redefine customer experiences, reinvent business models, and fundamentally alter how markets operate.
Instead of asking:
“How can AI make our current processes more efficient?”
Organisations should be asking:
“How will AI change the economics of competition in our industry?”
This shift in perspective moves AI from being an operational initiative to becoming a strategic capability.
Companies that embrace this transition will not simply work faster — they will compete differently.
The Five AI Capabilities Defining the Future of Marketing
As marketing evolves into an AI-native function, five foundational capabilities are emerging.
1. Continuous Insights
Traditional marketing relies on periodic surveys, historical reporting, and static segmentation.

AI enables an always-on intelligence engine that continuously gathers customer signals, analyses sentiment, builds synthetic audiences, predicts emerging needs, and informs decision-making in real time.
Insights become continuous rather than occasional.
2. Scaled Creativity
Creative production is no longer limited by human capacity.
Agentic creative systems can generate, evaluate, optimise, and deploy thousands of brand-consistent content variations while continuously learning from performance.
Creativity shifts from campaign-based execution to an adaptive operating system.
3. Hyperpersonalization
Traditional personalisation segments customers into predefined groups.
AI enables dynamic one-to-one experiences where every customer journey is individually optimised based on behaviour, context, intent, and predicted needs.
Every interaction becomes uniquely relevant.
4. Marketing to AI Agents
Marketing is no longer directed solely at humans.
Increasingly, purchasing decisions are influenced — or even made — by large language models and autonomous AI agents.
Brands must therefore optimise not only for search engines and human audiences but also for machine interpretation, trust, discoverability, and recommendation.
The future customer may be an AI agent acting on behalf of a human.
5. Always-on Orchestration
Marketing has traditionally operated through periodic planning cycles.
AI replaces this with continuous orchestration.
Campaigns, budgets, media allocation, customer journeys, and channel performance are optimised dynamically using real-time feedback, historical learning, and autonomous decision-making.
Marketing becomes a living system rather than a sequence of campaigns.
The Shift Ahead
These capabilities represent more than incremental improvements.
Together, they redefine how marketing creates value.
Organisations that continue measuring AI solely by productivity gains may achieve short-term efficiency, but they are unlikely to build a sustainable competitive advantage.

Those that redesign marketing around continuous intelligence, autonomous creativity, personalised experiences, AI-native discovery, and real-time orchestration will be positioned to compete in fundamentally different ways.
The question is no longer whether AI will transform marketing.
The question is whether your marketing organisation is evolving quickly enough to compete in an AI-native economy.
As these capabilities mature, marketing itself changes — and so do the people responsible for running it.

The next wave of competitive advantage will come not only from new technologies, but from new roles designed to orchestrate them. As marketing becomes AI-native, the final advantage will belong to organisations that redesign how people, systems, and decisions work together.

children.text: The tectonic plates of customer experience are shifting, and the epicenter? Artificial Intelligence. This isn’t a gentle tremor; it’s a full-blown seismic event reshaping the very landscape of engagement. We’re not talking about chatbots and automated replies; we’re witnessing the dawn of a hyper-intelligent, emotionally attuned era of customer interaction. Are you poised to ride this wave, or will you be swept away by its force?
AI-powered customer experience is no longer a roadmap item; it’s the new baseline.
Data Speaks: The Oracle Has Spoken.
Let’s dispense with the hypotheticals and dive into the irrefutable truth: AI is no longer a futuristic whisper, it’s the roaring engine of contemporary business.
Nearly Half of Tech Leaders (49%) Have Crossed the AI Rubicon:
This isn’t a trial run; it’s a full-scale integration. The message is clear: AI is no longer optional.
Indian CEOs See Profitability Surge (51%):
In a market defined by rapid growth and fierce competition, Generative AI isn’t just a tool, it’s a profit multiplier.
Real Revenue, Real Impact (36%):
This isn’t theoretical; it’s tangible growth, directly attributable to the power of Gen AI. The age of speculation is over; the age of demonstrable results is here.
These figures aren’t just numbers; they’re a clarion call. The AI revolution isn’t coming; it’s already here, and it’s rewriting the rules of the game.
The Customer: A Digital Nomad with Exquisite Demands.
Today’s customer isn’t just a consumer; they’re a discerning digital nomad, demanding experiences that transcend the ordinary. They expect:
Preemptive Service: The Power of Prescience:
They crave solutions before they even articulate the problem, demanding a level of anticipation that borders on telepathy.
Hyper-Personalization: The Art of the Individual:
They expect experiences tailored to their unique digital fingerprint, a symphony of personalized interactions.
Emotional Resonance: The Language of Feeling:
They seek brands that understand their unspoken emotions, forging connections that resonate on a deeper level.
Omnichannel Orchestration: The Symphony of Seamlessness:
They demand a consistent, fluid experience across every touchpoint, a seamless journey through the digital ecosystem.
To meet these elevated expectations, businesses must wield AI like a master craftsman, sculpting experiences that are not just efficient, but profoundly human.
Unleashing the AI Kraken: Key Strategic Imperatives.
AI as the Architect of CX Renaissance:
AI isn’t just a tool; it’s a catalyst for a customer experience renaissance. It enables the creation of dynamic, responsive ecosystems that anticipate needs and exceed expectations.
The Ethical Compass: Navigating the AI Frontier:
Trust is the currency of the future. Responsible AI adoption, anchored in ethical principles and robust governance, is non-negotiable.
Empowering the Human Element: The AI-Augmented Workforce:
AI isn’t about replacing humans; it’s about empowering them. By automating the mundane, AI frees up human potential for creativity, empathy, and strategic problem-solving.
AI-Driven Business Alchemy: Forging New Paradigms:
AI is the alchemist of modern business, transforming traditional models into agile, customer-centric ecosystems like quick commerce and XaaS.
Beyond the Algorithm: The Soul of CX.

While AI provides the scaffolding, the human element remains the soul of customer experience. Humanized AI, capable of understanding and responding to emotional nuances, is crucial. But equally important is the strategic integration of human interaction, ensuring that technology enhances, rather than replaces, the human touch.
The Call to Action: Crafting Your AI Legacy.
To truly harness the transformative power of AI, businesses must adopt a strategic, culturally nuanced approach. This involves:
Developing a visionary AI strategy that aligns with core business objectives.
Building a robust data fortress, fortified by ethical governance.
Championing ethical AI practices, ensuring fairness and transparency.
Empowering your workforce with the tools and knowledge to thrive in the AI era.
Embracing a culture of continuous learning and optimization.
The AI revolution is not a spectator sport; it’s an active endeavor. Are you ready to architect your future?

children.text: This document explores the potential pitfalls of over-reliance on Artificial Intelligence (AI) in User Experience (UX) design, arguing that while AI offers efficiency and data-driven insights, it risks neglecting the crucial element of understanding the "why" behind user behavior. It examines how this shift could lead to homogenized experiences and a decline in truly innovative UX solutions, emphasizing the continued importance of human empathy and qualitative research in the design process. We will also touch on how a UI UX design agency like can help balance AI-driven insights with human-centered design principles.
At its core, this is a question about AI and UX research: whether faster answers are costing us a deeper understanding of people.
The Rise of AI in UX

AI is rapidly transforming the landscape of UX design. From automated A/B testing and personalized recommendations to AI-powered design tools, the technology promises to streamline workflows, optimize user interfaces, and create more engaging experiences. AI algorithms can analyze vast datasets of user behavior, identify patterns, and predict user preferences with remarkable accuracy. This data-driven approach allows designers to make informed decisions, optimize conversion rates, and personalize experiences at scale.

However, this reliance on data and algorithms raises a critical question: are we sacrificing the depth of understanding that comes from qualitative research and human empathy? Are we becoming so focused on optimizing for efficiency that we are losing sight of the "why" behind user behavior?
The Danger of Data Without Understanding

AI excels at identifying what users are doing, but it often struggles to explain why they are doing it. For example, an AI algorithm might identify that users are abandoning a checkout process at a specific step. It can even suggest potential solutions, such as simplifying the form or offering a discount. However, it may not be able to tell you why users are abandoning the process. Are they concerned about security? Are they confused by the shipping options? Are they simply distracted?

Without understanding the underlying motivations and emotions driving user behavior, designers risk implementing solutions that address the symptoms but not the root cause. This can lead to a cycle of iterative optimization that improves metrics without fundamentally enhancing the user experience.
The Importance of Qualitative Research
Qualitative research methods, such as user interviews, ethnographic studies, and usability testing, provide invaluable insights into the "why" behind user behavior. These methods allow designers to:
Develop Empathy:
By directly interacting with users, designers can gain a deeper understanding of their needs, frustrations, and motivations.
Uncover Hidden Insights:
Qualitative research can reveal unexpected patterns and insights that might be missed by quantitative data analysis.
Generate Innovative Ideas:
By understanding the underlying reasons for user behavior, designers can generate more creative and effective solutions.
Contextualize Data:
Qualitative research provides context for quantitative data, helping designers to interpret the numbers and understand the story behind them.
The Risk of Homogenization

One of the biggest concerns about the increasing use of AI in UX design is the potential for homogenization. AI algorithms are trained on existing data, which means they are inherently biased towards the status quo. If designers rely solely on AI-driven insights, they risk creating experiences that are similar to everything else on the market.

True innovation requires a willingness to challenge assumptions, experiment with new ideas, and push the boundaries of what is possible. This requires a human-centered approach that prioritizes understanding the unique needs and aspirations of users.
Balancing AI and Human-Centered Design

The key to successful UX design in the age of AI is to find a balance between data-driven insights and human empathy. AI should be used as a tool to augment, not replace, the human design process. Designers should:
Use AI to identify patterns and trends in user behavior.
Conduct qualitative research to understand the "why" behind those patterns.
Use AI to test and optimize design solutions.
Continuously iterate and refine designs based on user feedback.
A
UI UX design agency

like WUGWEB can play a crucial role in helping organizations navigate this balance. They bring expertise in both AI-driven insights and human-centered design principles, ensuring that technology is used to enhance, not diminish, the user experience. They can help organizations:
Develop a comprehensive UX strategy that integrates AI and human-centered design.
Conduct user research to understand the needs and motivations of their target audience.
Design and develop user interfaces that are both efficient and engaging.
Test and optimize designs using both quantitative and qualitative methods.
Conclusion

AI has the potential to revolutionize UX design, but it is important to be aware of the potential pitfalls. By focusing solely on data and algorithms, we risk losing sight of the "why" behind user behavior and creating homogenized experiences that fail to meet the unique needs of users. To avoid this, designers must embrace a human-centered approach that prioritizes empathy, qualitative research, and a willingness to challenge assumptions. By balancing AI-driven insights with human understanding, we can create truly innovative and impactful UX solutions.

children.text: The zero-UI and why it is crucial to the future of design.
For better or worse, much design work is still visual these days. This makes sense since the essential products we interact with have screens.
Television introduced us to screens in 1938 for the first time. Ever since, our world has been flooded with Computers, iPods, smartphones, tablets… and more and more types of screen-based devices.
Hence, today only a minute goes by without interacting with a screen.
The Internet of Things,
coined by Kevin Ashton in 1999
, surrounds us with intelligent
devices
. In 2020 more than 10 billion devices were already connected to the Internet — and by 2025,
this amount is expected to double up to 20 billion.
So, knowing that intelligent machines can hear our words, anticipate our needs, and sense our gestures, what does that mean for the future of design, especially as those screens go away?
Let’s discover together what this so-called Zero-UI stands for. 👇🏻
What is Zero-UI?
Zero User Interface, or Zero-UI, is an increasingly popular concept first coined by designer
Andy Goodman
, formerly at Accenture Interactive’s agency.
It isn’t a new idea. I bet you are already familiar with it.

Have you ever used an Amazon Echo, talked to your iPhone using Siri, or skipped a song, double-tipping your AirPods? Then, you’ve already used a device that could be considered part of this so-called Zero-UI concept!

It is about getting away from the touchscreen and interfacing with the devices around us more naturally. This includes different fields such as haptics, computer vision, voice control, and even artificial intelligence.
Why do we need this transition?
To understand the need for this transition let’s look at how we currently communicate with technology to understand the need for this transition. Most of us interact with our devices daily through a
Graphical User Interface (GUI)

A GUI interface allows users to interact with electronic devices through graphical icons and visual indicators. It can be a displaying screen — for computers — or a touchscreen for any kind of phone or tablet. Thus, users must still use a mouse and keyboard combination or tapping and swiping to transmit information.
If you look at the history of computing, starting with the jacquard loom in 1801, humans have always had to interact with machines abstractly and complexly. — by Andy Goodman.

To be fair, interfaces have come a long way from their humble origins, but they still have yet to provide the best experiences for those who use them. We download an endless amount of apps and click through too many screens in an attempt to perform daily tasks.

Luckily, designers and developers are addressing the issue to bring forth some exciting changes to help out with this problem. Just like computers evolved from being used via running code in a terminal to having a friendly and intuitive graphical interface, the next natural step has no interface.

Today, machines still force us to come to them on their terms, speaking their language. The next step for electronic devices is to finally understand us on our terms, in our own natural words, behaviours, and gestures.

This is precisely where Zero-UI appears. It is aimed to allow more natural interactions when compared to screen-based devices. At the helm of this transition are both gesture-based and voice-recognition user interfaces.
According to
Dharmik
the gaming world has been one of the first

to adopt gesture controls to provide a more natural user experience. The Nintendo Wii console was launched in 2006 and already contains gesture-based controllers or later models. You can watch the revolutionary launch of Wii advertising below!
Launching advertising of Wii.
Voice recognition is another common Zero-UI feature found in our daily life. During the 2000s, Google launched Google Voice Search. Until Alexa was first released in 2014, voice
recognition experienced a commercial explosion.
Ever since, more than 312 million Alexa devices have been sold. Amazon is expected to overpass this amount by 2025:
320 million are expected to be sold.
The world seems to have fallen for the charm of this so-called Zero-UI, which will not likely change.
How will Zero-UI change the design?

According to Andy Goodman, Zero-UI represents a whole new dimension for designers. He compares the designer’s leap from UI to Zero-UI as just designing for two sizes to thinking about what a user tries to do in any possible workflow.

Instead of relying on clicking, typing and tapping, users will now input information utilising voice, gestures, and touch. Interactions will move away from phones and computers and into physical devices. We will communicate instead.
The most important — and revolutionary — part of this concept is that it can be used for cities, homes, ecosystems, and personal devices.
So, this technology does — and will —
create a massive effect on society.
Different Types of Zero-UI
There are various ways to communicate with current technology instead of relying on a visual screen, which can be used to achieve this desired Zero-UI.
I. Voice Recognition and Control

It’s a process where software or device identifies the human voice, understands some instruction, and performs a particular action accordingly. When a user asks a question or gives a statement to the software, the tool recognises and reacts to the user’s query.
The best examples of voice recognition and control are Siri and Amazon Echo.
II. Haptic Feedback

Haptic Feedback facilitates users with vibration-based feedback. Even though we are already used to it when interacting with our phones, it is an integral part of wearable products such as fitness trackers and smartwatches as they enable users with notifications. It is also an essential feature for current game controllers — you can notice someone attacking you before seeing it on screen.
In the coming future,
it will also be available with intelligent clothing.
III. Ambient

Ambient devices create a bridge between digital and physical space. It works on the principle of glanceability, where there is no need to open notifications and applications. Ambient device-based interactions are connected and offer a browserless experience. The best example would be controlling our house devices using Alexa or Google Home.
IV. Gesture-Based User Interface

It is one of the most natural ways of interaction. The gaming world first adopted this concept. It allows users to incorporate more motion and physical space properties than just button-based commands. The best examples of a gesture-based user interface are Microsoft Kinect, Think Wii, and PlayStation Move.
Google’s Project Soli.
Google has also released a gesture control product Project, Soli. A sensing technology detects touchless gesture interaction using a small radar.
V. Context Awareness
Contextually aware apps and devices facilitate users with a more simplified physical and digital experience by anticipating their needs. It eliminates all additional layers of interaction.

The AirPods are one of the best examples. By introducing sensors into a device or location data, we can design next-generation contextual experience that offers more implicit interaction rather than explicit.
These are some of the most common — and already working — ways to communicate with technology. Upcoming times will introduce breakthrough devices with these outstanding capabilities and even more.
Zero-UI will rely on Data and AI.
Whereas interface designers right now live in apps like InDesign and Adobe Illustrator, the non-linear design problems of Zero-UI will require vastly different tools and skill sets.
“Designers will have to become experts in science, biology, and psychology to create these devices… stuff we don’t have to think about when screens constrain our designs.”— Andy Goodman.

As we move away from screens, many of our interfaces will have to become more automatic, anticipatory, and predictive. One clear example would be designing a TV controller. Depending on who is standing in front of that TV, the gestures it needs to understand to do something as simple as turn up the volume might be radically different: a 40-year-old might twist an imaginary dial in mid-air, while a millennial might jerk their thumb up.
What’s after Zero-UI?

Zero-UI is the ultra-modern version of artificial intelligence. Zero-UI is meant to allow users to experience more human-like interactions. Soon Google Assistant, Siri and Alexa will become the memories of the precious past of the tech world.
Looking to the future, the next big step will be for the concept of the ‘device’ to disappear. — by Sundar Pichai, Google C.E.O

children.text: Landmark Group (with brands like Max Fashion and Splash) is the leading fashion retailer in the middle east and gulf region. While the sales of these brands inside malls and offline stores have been growing year or year, the sales from online channels (Eg
Maxfashion.com
) have declined. It is principal because customers only get to try the products after purchase (to check the fabric, the fit and the overall look) and hence are reluctant to buy stuff online.
This fashion ecommerce UX case study walks through how I approached that problem, from research and assumptions to flows and UI.
The Problem

Landmark has decided to build a new and independent fashion e-commerce app. This app shows a limited customer set of products (approx. 500), but the key differentiator is that customers can get these products on the same day for a trial (less than 2 hours). The customer has to pay a nominal fee of 7 AED per product as a trial fee (Which has to be paid upfront. Cash on Delivery is not allowed for trial fee payment). Once delivered, the customer can try all the clothes ordered and decide to buy or reject each product. Customers will have 30 minutes to try all the products while the delivery guy waits. If the customer chooses to buy a product (let’s assume the selling price is 100 AED), the trial fee is waived and adjusted in the product cost. The customer can then pay the changed amount (AED 93) online on the app or via cash to the delivery guy. The rejected items will return to the delivery guy.
The Task
To create Basic Design Guidelines including Typography, Color Palette
To design Product Details Page (PDP), Cart or Bag Screen (where a bunch of products is added for trial)
To create Post-order journey screens (tracking after order after placement, rejecting or accepting the products post-trial and making payments for accepted products)
To create Information Design and Hierarchy (Communicate the entire Trial Model, Trial Fees, Conditions)

To begin with, I needed to build my case. One needs to start making a product. Getting all these insights before embarking on the design is critical to ensure that the team solves the correct problems and is aligned with the project goals.
The flowchart below outlines the core stages of my redesign process. I chose to take an iterative approach, testing and improving the design throughout.

body.alt: My approach: exercised in five parts
body.caption: My approach: exercised in five parts

children.text: A bit more details…
Discover — How do users shop online and in-store?

To thoroughly investigate the problem space of online shopping, I conducted observations in stores and online for fashion brands and other competitors. And then, I conducted interviews based on topic maps. Next, I coded users’ responses by looking for commonalities in the challenges users faced and their contexts.
What people love in store
First-hand experience with the product (touch and see)
Staff accessible when needed
The environment made room for people to explore and be inspired
What people love online
Can look at lots of items quickly
Save items to list
Able to check product details and availability online

body.alt: The placement of the product I want to create
body.caption: The placement of the product I want to create

children.text: Understanding User
My principle is “Start With Why” to understand why users would need this app. Why should they care? It establishes the context and can help identify the problem users are facing.
We ask why to find purpose. It guides the narrative and defines the value proposition.

body.alt: This model helps us think. I understand that there are other models, and this one might be controversial.
body.caption: This model helps us think. I understand that there are other models, and this one might be controversial.

children.text: When designing for international markets, having a more international sample often reveals problems that could well exist for domestic users, too. We found that there were no distinct differences between cultures when it comes to main usability issues such as navigation. It resonates with this finding by Jacob Nielsen:

“People are the same the world over, and all the usability guidelines remain the same. After all, usability guidelines are derived from the principles of human computer interaction (HCI), which are founded on the characteristics of computers and the human brain and the many ways the two differ.”

body.alt: UAE is a highly diverse society
body.caption: UAE is a highly diverse society

children.text: First, I created a provisional persona for a typical user based on online research and the base of users within my friends and family. (If this were a more significant project, I would want to validate it with more user interviews.) this persona was created with assumptions and not fully research-based, but it was something that I came back to throughout my project to guide my design decisions and priorities.
Job Stories
I used the Jobs To Be Done framework to explore a context where users would use it and understand their motivation and desired outcome.
It culminated in artefacts called Job Stories:
Usability Tests + User Interview
I opted to validate my assumptions by usability testing further and interviewing a comparative demographic: millennials, online shoppers who are users of Amazon, Zara, Myntra, H&M, etc.
Assumption #1
A significant portion of users who reach the home screen intend to buy specific items.
Findings: Answers collected to support the assumption that there is a significant portion of users who shop online only when they have purchase intent for a specific item(s):
Assumption #2
Users with specific items in mind look forward to having the option to try the fit and fabric as well.
Findings: Users’ behaviour in response to the above scenarios further validates assumption #2, as users with purchase intent will go for significantly more than place an order online.
Assumption #3
Time is taken to try apparel by a user (as discussed by a group of 10 females)
Findings: User’s time requirement to try an outfit varies with the item, and if they are trying to create a match.

body.alt: Standard time is measured to try an item. Icon: Flaticon
body.caption: Standard time is measured to try an item. Icon: Flaticon

children.text: Assumption #4
Many users are willing to pay for the products they order to try and later buy them.
Findings: I asked users if they were willing to pay for this service per product, to which most agreed — however, the behaviour was a bit confusing.
Defining Pain Points

People want to be able to quickly decide an outfit without compromising their creativity and sense of self. Statement pieces reflect personality. Individuals who have statement pieces, tie their identity with their outfits.
Pain Point 1

For a brand selling all lifestyle products, the possibility of products not qualifying for test fit is relatively high. I am making a collection of products based on availability for a home test fit. Assuming only some of the products will be eligible.
Pain Point 2
Making a single Order Id for both: products for test fit & products purchased instantly; e.g. the User has already purchased socks but wants to try out shoes
Pain Point 3

Identifying the time required to try the products ordered for fit — if feasible and finding a solution. Based on Assumption 3, the time will vary as per the order type — 3 t-shirts will take as much time as a Dress.
Pain Point 4
Tracking the entire order, time calculation and triumphant purchase/return of products. The clarity in logistic ops is a must.
To help prioritize the issues, I used a 2x2 map to help rank the category of the problems by how important they are to the business (x-axis) and the users (y-axis).
Ideation
To understand more, I made a quick process map — focussing more on the order part and less on the User navigation while exploring.
I had to remember the multiple use cases where the User will buy/test-fit or both and the time & fee adjustment accordingly.
I should play with toggle buttons for the Test Fit feature and not disrupt the Law of Similarity.

body.alt: Explorations- utilizing the cart page and reducing the steps
body.caption: Explorations- utilizing the cart page and reducing the steps

children.text: UI — Making the product scalable for Arabic

Knowing that the product is targeted at Arabic and non-Arabic, I had to make it scalable for two design versions: English and Arabic. Of course, I first designed the English version, which can adapt to the Arabic UI by mirroring the design right-to-left (RTL). But when creating specifically for Arab users, it’s not enough to just reflect the design. There are some local-specific usability considerations to apply.

body.alt: While the man to the right is running from right to left, the story was intended to be read from left to right
body.caption: While the man to the right is running from right to left, the story was intended to be read from left to right

children.text: While the man to the right is running from right to left, I’m pretty sure the story was intended to be read from left to right… Source:
http://gosmellthecoffee.com/archives/9570
Here are a few good examples from UXbert:
Copy and type:
Using screen real estate smartly:
Arabic is a “wordier” language; therefore, it might take up more space. I had to keep this in mind when designing the layout and UI element pixel size.
Paying attention to legibility:

Arabic characters are very complex; they have overhanging and looping features. The type needs to be at least four points larger than the corresponding English type to achieve the same degree of legibility. I also had to avoid bold and italics for the same reason.
Reading pattern:
Mirrored F-shape:
Arabic-speaking users mirror the F-shaped reading behaviour, so they had to put the most relevant information on top, as many left-to-right (LTR) sites do.
Mirroring icons:
Even in RTL websites, specific icons and logos should retain their LTR alignment, such as:
Icons that indicate direction: e.g. play or rewind buttons on media players, progress indicators, and a clock’s hands should constantly rotate clockwise too;
Icons that represent objects usually held with the right hand (e.g. phone icon);
Any words are written in other languages and Hindu-Arabic numerals (1,2,3, etc.);
Icons with user expectations: consider whether the hero has a user expectation to look a certain way. Also, changing the icon’s alignment would change its meaning.
Images:
had to make sure that the photos were culturally appropriate for target users

body.alt: The alignment is correct. Only the location of the icons is reversed
body.caption: The alignment is correct. Only the location of the icons is reversed

children.text: The alignment is correct. Notice that only the location of the icons is reversed; the alignment remains the same, adapting to user expectations.
Since it was just a task — I just did the English version keeping in mind the product need to be scalable for an Arabic version when required.

Continuing with the UI, I kept the category page similar to the standard eCommerce layout to avoid confusing the User. Saving a filter for Home try-on if the User is focussed is pretty sure to try before buying whatever the item is.

body.alt: Category page & filters product page and bag
body.caption: Category page & filters product page and bag

children.text: A solution to keep both — the normal and Test fit products in a single card as discussed in the pain points, hence the toggle button will help me identify the development and its different lifecycle.
If there is no product for a test fit, the User will proceed with the regular checkout.
Selecting the timing is critical since the task mentioned the delivery to be in hours — I am not using the date selection here, assuming it is for the same day.
Terms & Conditions are very critical here:
Based on Assumptions, the following things are to keep in mind
The user can try X number of products in Y time. This has been researched. Based on product selected, if the time calculations exceed Y time, further selection of products to be denied

In case we want to exceed time Y to Y1, the price of the product selected should increase; this is to ward off any constraint on demand & supply line. The price can go from AED3.00 to AED 4.00 if the time 30 minutes exceeds to 45 minutes
A limitation on products for test fit is must — based on previous research, no more than 3 dresses, or 6 t shirts etc can be selected for test fit. This data will come from more research
Safekeeping of product packaging — all tags and packaging must be kept as is it in case of a return, otherwise, a penalty is to be charged.
The User can edit the information before confirming the order

body.alt: standard checkout tracking and confirming the order
body.caption: standard checkout tracking and confirming the order

children.text: The User can easily track the order on the Map; in case there is no in-app navigation — a button to navigate it to maps is there. Once the order is received in other countries — I might have gone with a confirmation OTP, but not for the markets of the Middle East.
Upon a successful trial, the User can simply use the toggle to accept or reject the product.
The final price payable will be calculated accordingly — and based on that the User will proceed to the payment page or give cash on delivery.
Further…
While working on this, multiple scenarios came into my mind, but since they were not part of the task, I had to ignore them.
Why not a 3d Try on for fashion accessories?
The time of test fit will vary with age and gender as well — how will we quantify this information?

Doing case studies brings so many thoughts for me, always. I’d love to share my new findings with you guys. However, the solution in the actual project will vary significantly regarding the data we get from each version of the iteration and testing.
Note: I do not work for or affiliated with Landmark. This UX study was done to understand the problem and deliver a solution in 4 days.
