children.text: Recently I was tasked to study the Buyer's Dashboard, identify the pain points and the experience, and suggest changes. Though a big name, the job was enjoyable as Indiamart often tends to ignore the User for product visibility.
This IndiaMart UX case study walks through how I approached it, from research to the final dashboard concept.
Objective
Design of Buyer Dashboard to manage purchase requirements and improve supplier communication.
Background

Indiamart is a platform where businesses can list themselves and their products. Users can browse the products, look for an appropriate supplier, and connect with them for their requirements. Users can connect with suppliers by sending them a direct inquiry or alternatively they can post their requirement on IndiaMART and then we send them the details of the suitable suppliers. Users can enhance their profile by adding points like name, email id, image, etc. Our users register on the platform when they share their mobile numbers with us.
Task
My task was to recreate the Buyer's Dashboard covering
Managing past requirements
Post new requirements
Manage communication with suppliers
Analyze the requirements
Propose more features based on the pain points

I set out to improve the customer experience by reducing as much friction as possible from the buying & selling process on the IndiaMart website. This was done through deliberate, incremental changes to the design that considered both User and business objectives.
The Process
I followed IDEO's Human-Centered Design and Lean UX Design Thinking process to make sure that my design decisions were supported by user research and feedback.
Throughout the process, I've also constantly ensured that I was cycling regularly between divergent and convergent thinking to ensure I was:
Keeping my mind open to exploring all possible solutions
Keeping check of business objectives and general feasibility
I also considered BJ Fogg's Behavioral Model, which illustrates UX's impact on changing user behaviour. I aimed to ensure users could achieve their goals quickly (ability).
Empathising with the User
Provisional Personas

First, I created a provisional persona for a typical user for IndiaMart based on online research and the base of users within my friends and family. (If this were a more extensive project, I would want to validate with more user interviews.) this persona was created with assumptions and not fully research-based, but it was something that I came back to throughout my project to guide my design decisions and priorities.
Job Stories
I used the Jobs To Be Done framework to explore a context in which a user would use IndiaMart and understand their motivation and desired outcome.
This culminated in artefacts called Job Stories:

body.alt: 4 Job Stories for Dev, the Buyer Persona
body.caption: 4 Job Stories for Dev, the Buyer Persona

children.text: Defining the Problem

My beliefs about the time of IndiaMart were based on my analysis of their website and marketing materials. I prioritised each pain point based on its importance to the User as well as its importance to IndiaMart. My assumptions of the extent of users were based on conversations with existing and potential users.

body.alt: Prioritising pain points on a 2x2 matrix.
body.caption: Prioritising pain points on a 2x2 matrix.

children.text: I decided to tackle the pain points that were both important to users and IndiaMart. I redefined the pain points below.
Pain Point 1: Discoverability issue with the requirement

I attempted to post the condition for Strawberries on the existing portal. The details it asked for were all sorted. However, I was not allowed to select the supplier; the preferred supplier would connect me. Limits my choices here:
Pain Point 2: Recommendations not related to user/previous searches

The profile selection and search criteria give information on the industry the User is from; hence, the products on his Dashboard should be restricted to the user domain unless he searches explicitly for it.
It is a buyer's dashboard and not a general landing page.
Pain Point 3: Communication with Supplier issue

From my previous requirement, a supplier wanted to connect. However, I need help connecting with him directly via an IndiaMart portal connect-just the contacts were shared. Also, I need help editing my requirement once they are submitted.
There is a communication section which asks me to add a phone number. Is this for real?
Pain Point 4: The Dashboard UI was troublesome

We call it a Buyer's Dashboard. However, it presently is a search board and navigation that could be more visible/usable. I need help seeing my entire activity summary on a single screen. Much critical information needs to be included: Unread messages, Pending orders, Rejected/Pending requests, and a quick snapshot of the user profile.
The joke is 3 Search functionalities in the 1/3rd of the page. Wow!
Ideating the Solution

Based on the established pain points, I sketched multiple options to test and see how to optimise the user experience by initiating minimal changes. During the redesign process, I continued referring to the target audience, company mission, revenue model and my goal to focus on improving the user experience rather than making design changes. After a few rounds of iterations, I came to a good place with the solutions.
Before going for the Hi-fi, I wanted to make sure:
To keep the existing Top navigation menu, IndiaMART must have done it after some research.
Focussing on the Dashboard itself rather than going for the entire flow as this was just a minor assignment.
We are keeping the existing colour palette wherever possible.
Suggesting only rational changes — not a UI epitome
I did some preliminary validation on the Lo-Fi UI sketches and used the feedback to refine my sketches and narrow down my solutions for the Hi-Fi mockups.
UI & Prototype
“If a picture is worth 1000 words, a prototype is worth 1000 meetings.” — credited at IDEO

As mentioned, I retained the Top navigation menu. However, I changed the font to Muli. Also, I removed the top banner search and replaced it with a quick view of activities. The right side will show the payment protection information. A separate section was added to urge the User to update the profile w.r.t. the industry type and tags to display personalised recommendations.
There is so much which can be done with the Buyer's profile; tagging, company listing and delivery/order/payment tracking, which we will discuss in the following article.
TL;DR

IndiaMART is India's largest online B2B marketplace, connecting buyers with suppliers. Founded in 1999, the company's mission is 'to make doing business easy'. With a 60% market share of the online B2B Classified space in India, the channel focuses on providing a platform to Small & Medium Enterprises (SMEs), large enterprises, and individuals.
I hope you enjoyed the read and learned something new!
Note: I do not work for or affiliated with, IndiaMART. This UX study was done to help make me a better designer.

children.text: I was asked to study an e-commerce company: Desi Atta Company. They sell a wide range of flours and flour-based ready-mixes. They have developed an e-commerce website. Considering the competition, they want to change its look and feel to deliver a better user experience to its customers.
This grocery ecommerce UX case study walks through that redesign, with a focus on the mobile experience.
Introduction

Desi Atta Company is the first food collective in India to introduce a wide range of flours and flour-based ready-mixes from ancient Indian grains, millets & pulses. Their vision is to create a community of people who love to cook traditional and experimental dishes with flour. These ready-mixes and unique flours are only available offline, and hence a website to cater for the market, which is rich in delicacies surrounding cultural festivities/festivals.

body.alt: Banner on the website mentioning their USP
body.caption: Banner on the website mentioning their USP

children.text: The Brief

With the rise in e-commerce and hundreds of competitive websites, everyone wants UX personalization and the best approach. The company wanted me to look into the existing Product and enhance the mobile experience. I was explicitly asked to:
Suggest all the relevant points that can be practiced to enhance the mobile website.
There are a lot of negative/white spaces on the website. Suggest what all can be done to rectify it.
Do a complete analysis of the website and list down the points of improvement.
Suggest what new can be done to provide a delightful user experience.

To begin with, I needed to build my case. One needs to start redesigning a product. It takes time to understand how users use your product and their problems. Getting all these insights before embarking on the redesign is critical to ensure that the team solves the correct issues and is aligned with the project goals.
The flowchart below outlines the core stages of my redesign process. I chose to take an iterative approach, testing and improving the design throughout.
Understanding the Product
Product knowledge vs product understanding is similar to the contrast between features and benefits. And just as "features tell, benefits sell."

Indian food is one of the tastiest and subtest in the world. There is no homogeneity of flavour between North and South or East and West but rather a wealth of flavours, simply staggering tastes. Culinary diversity is one of India's treasures. There is so much to Indian cuisine that one should rather talk of "Indian Cuisines". Each region offers their distinctive culinary characteristics and numerous traditional dishes.

The flours are made of either grain or seeds(pseudo-grains like amaranth, millets, buckwheats etc.) and even from beans and lentils. These are used in different parts of the country for various purposes: fasting, celebration, health habits or religious ceremonies. Here is the list of Indian flours. The list is long w.r.t the demography and users. However, no list is complete, but you can Learn about Different Kinds of Flour.
I will summarise Desi Atta Company into a small chart for better understanding:

body.alt: The placement of Desi Atta Company
body.caption: The placement of Desi Atta Company

children.text: Understanding User
Step 1. Identify the Users
The first step is to identify the users of Desi Atta Company; their key characteristics, demographics, behaviours, attitudes, and goals.

The second step involves my objectives for this Research. This allows me to form a hypothesis that I can test with the users. These are why I'm conducting this Research and the insights I'm trying to get from it.
Step 2: Forming my Hypothesis

Desi Atta Company would aim to enjoy themselves with their families by eating more traditional, experimental, and healthy food. To be able to do so gives them a sense of fulfilment and happiness. For Desi Atta Company to be of more value, they need to curate specific solutions to specific worries of their customers. It's not simply adding more products but rather giving their customers something more they can value
Step 3: Defining the Persona
In this scenario, I am defining the persona of Nikita, 29, who lives in Gurgaon and often prepares meals.
Going further into her personality, this is how we can further define:

Desi Atta Company's current site carries products, a few non-tailored recipes and a blog which could be more visible. For them to stand out in the saturated market, keep their customers loyal, and acquire new customers, Desi Atta must extend itself beyond a flour store and be able to give more value to their customers by providing educational talks, tours, curated recipes or meal courses, community gatherings and such.
Step 4: User Narratives

This stage of the process will focus on the users' narratives. These are ideal scenarios of the interaction between the User and the website, which will guide us in building our wireframes later. To construct the records, I'm using this funnel as a guide:
Existing Research
I researched and found existing studies that would validate (or invalidate) the assumptions, as the validity would influence the design decisions made to address the needs of the User:
Assumption #1
A significant portion of users who reach the home screen intend to buy specific items.
Research findings:

Research data suggests that millennials make up most purchase intenders, and roughly half do not browse online for entertainment shopping. Assuming this is true of Desi Atta Company users, then it is likely that a significant portion of users landing on the home screen intends to purchase a specific item(s).
Research data:
Millennials (ages 21–34) make up 49%-59% of global purchase intenders who browse online and 52%-63% of those who buy online
Almost 50% of millennials regularly browse through items online for entertainment; the remainder do not
In 2018, 79% of APAC millennials reported purchasing goods online within the last 12 months, significantly more than the general population.
Assumption #2
Users with specific items in mind to be purchased will usually opt to use the search bar
Research findings:

In Research performed by Stanford University and Pinterest personnel around almost 3 million Pinterest users and their browsing/ purchasing behaviour, it was found that users with built-up purchase intent exhibit more searching and click-through behaviour at the expense of browsing and content saving
Usability Tests + User Interview

Without access to the Desi Atta Company user base, I opted to validate my assumptions by usability testing further and interviewing a comparative demographic: millennials, online shoppers who are users of amazon pantry, growers, big basket etc.
Assumption #1
A significant portion of users who reach the home screen intend to buy specific items.
Findings: Answers collected to support the assumption that there is a significant portion of users who shop online only when they have purchase intent for a specific item(s):
Assumption #2
Users with specific items to purchase will opt to use the search bar.
Findings: Users' behaviour in response to the above scenarios further validates assumption #2, as users with purchase intent used "search" significantly more than "browse."
Assumption #3
Content on the Homescreen lacks personalization and relevance
Findings: I ran users through scenarios that encouraged browsing during testing and followed up with questions about the relevance of content presented on the home screen:
Research Summary
Most buyers may use the search bar more often than explore because they have purchase intent for specific items.
Homescreen content can be more personalized for most users tested
User Journey Maps

Leveraging my understanding of user behaviours from Research and empathy, I created a journey map depicting expected behaviour exhibited by e-commerce shoppers. Doing so helped me visualize which areas needed improvement so that I could map potential solutions to them.
Solution
Based on the data I had from the Research, I worked on some wireframes while removing things that were not essential to the Product and adding more filters to enhance the experience.
There were a couple of things I tweaked, namely:
Added product filters in the menu section
Removed filters from the cateogry pages, as the number of products were less.
Enhanced the product images to utilise the white space
Added recipe, information and nutrient value
Changed the fonts
The image below is tentative and contains only some suggestions, but it is selective due to a lack of time. Login/payment/checkout issues are not uploaded here.
Conclusion

Although the project succeeded, we only had time to explore some of our ideas. Much can be done in this product w.r.t. recipe and Product added together and blended with a campaign or a referral program, an interactive community etc.

This project also reinforced the importance of iterated usability testing and its significance in designing good user experiences. Doing the competitive analysis was also tremendously helpful in helping me understand the value of knowing usability conventions and seeing how they can be employed or improved upon to help small businesses thrive in a vast global marketplace.
This is for research purpose only, I am not involved with Desi Atta Company directly.

docs.aiSummary: Covers identifying and reducing UX debt.

children.text: UX debt slows teams just like technical debt.

Every product team knows the feeling. A feature shipped with a temporary workaround. A settings page grew one toggle at a time until nobody could find anything. Two flows that do the same thing look completely different. None of these were disasters on their own, but together they make the product harder to use and harder to change. That's UX debt.
Like technical debt, it isn't always a mistake to take on. Sometimes shipping fast is the right call. The problem comes when the debt is invisible, nobody tracks it, and the interest keeps adding up.
What UX debt actually is
It is the gap between the experience your product delivers today and the experience it should deliver, created by past decisions, shortcuts and neglect. It shows up as:
Inconsistency.
Different patterns for the same action, mismatched styles and wording.
Friction.
Extra steps, confusing labels, unclear errors and dead ends.
Accessibility gaps.
Missing labels, poor contrast and keyboard traps.
Outdated flows.
Journeys designed for an older version of the product or a different user base.
Orphaned features.
Things that exist, confuse people and that nobody owns.
How it builds up
It rarely comes from one bad decision. It accumulates quietly through everyday pressures:
Deadlines.
A launch date forces a "we'll fix it later" design that never gets revisited.
Feature layering.
New capabilities are bolted onto existing screens without rethinking the whole.
Team changes.
People leave, context is lost, and new teams build on top of patterns they don't fully understand.
No shared system.
Without common components and guidelines, every team solves the same problem differently.
Skipped research.
Assumptions go untested, and small usability problems become baked in.
The cost grows over time. Users work around problems, support teams answer the same questions, and designers and engineers spend extra effort on every change because the foundation is messy.
How to spot it
You can't pay down what you can't see. Look for evidence in several places:
Support tickets and chat logs.
Repeated questions about the same feature often point straight at a design problem.
Usability testing.
Watching a handful of users attempt common tasks reveals friction quickly.
Analytics.
Drop-offs in key flows, unused features and high error rates are useful signals.
Heuristic review.
A structured walkthrough against known usability principles surfaces inconsistencies.
Team feedback.
Designers, engineers and support staff often know exactly where the pain is. Ask them.
Log what you find in a single debt backlog. For each item, note what the problem is, where it appears, who it affects and what evidence supports it.
How to prioritize it
Not all debt deserves attention right away. Score each item on a few simple dimensions:
User impact.
How many people hit it, and how badly does it affect them?
Business impact.
Does it touch revenue, retention, support load or compliance?
Effort.
How much design and engineering work would fixing it take?
Risk.
Does it create accessibility, legal or trust issues?

High-impact, low-effort items are your quick wins. High-impact, high-effort items need planning and a clear case for investment. Low-impact items can wait, or be fixed opportunistically when a team is already working nearby.
How to pay it down
Paying it down works best as a steady habit, not a one-time cleanup.
Reserve capacity.
Set aside a regular share of each sprint or cycle for debt work, so it doesn't compete with every new feature.
Fix as you go.
When a team touches an area for new work, include nearby debt in the scope.
Invest in a design system.
Shared components and patterns prevent new inconsistencies and make fixes easier to roll out.
Retire what doesn't work.
Removing an unused or confusing feature is often the fastest improvement you can make.
Make it visible.
Share the backlog with product and engineering leads, and report progress so the work gets credit.
Preventing new debt

Some debt is inevitable, but you can reduce how fast it grows. Include design review in your definition of done. Test key flows with users before launch, even informally. Write down why decisions were made so future teams have context. And when you do take a shortcut on purpose, log it immediately with a plan to revisit.
Treat it like any other debt

UX debt is real, and it compounds. The good news is that it's manageable once you can see it. Make it visible, prioritize by impact, reserve time to pay it down and build habits that stop it piling up. Your users will notice the difference, and so will the team building the product.

children.text: Understand where your UX organization stands.

Every company does UX in some form, even if nobody calls it that. Someone decides how a screen works, how a form flows, what an error message says. What differs is how deliberately that work happens, who does it, and how much it influences decisions. A UX maturity model gives you a way to describe those differences and, more usefully, a way to see what comes next.

Several published models exist, and they use different names and numbers of stages. The details vary, but the overall shape is broadly similar. Below is a practical way to think about UX maturity, followed by how to move from one stage to the next.
The stages of UX maturity
1. Absent

UX isn't recognized as a discipline. Interfaces are designed by whoever is building them, usually engineers or product managers working from requirements. Nobody talks to users directly, and decisions are based on opinion or the loudest voice in the room.
2. Emerging

A few people care about user experience and start doing it on their own. Maybe a designer is hired, or a developer runs a few informal usability tests. The work is valuable but fragile. It depends on individuals, has no budget, and often happens late in the process when changes are expensive.
3. Structured

UX becomes a recognized function with dedicated people. There's a design process, some research happens before building, and early versions of shared patterns or a design system appear. However, UX is still often treated as a service: teams bring it in to make things look good rather than to shape what gets built.
4. Integrated

UX is part of how products are planned and delivered. Designers and researchers sit in product teams from the start. Research informs roadmaps, not just screens. Leaders understand the value of UX and fund it consistently. Metrics include user-centered measures alongside business ones.
5. User-driven

User understanding shapes strategy across the organization. Executives ask about user evidence before major decisions. Research insights are shared widely and reused. Teams across the business, including support, sales and operations, contribute to and act on what's learned about users. UX is no longer a department's job; it's how the company works.
How to tell where you are
Honest assessment is the first step. Ask your team questions like these:
When was the last time a decision was changed because of user research?
Do designers join projects at the start, or after requirements are set?
Is there a dedicated budget for research and design, or is it borrowed?
Do leaders talk about users in planning meetings without being prompted?
Can someone outside the design team find past research findings?
Most organizations sit across two stages at once. One product team might be integrated while another is still emerging. That's normal. Assess at the team level as well as the company level.
Moving from absent to emerging

The first move is simply making user evidence visible. Run a few lightweight usability sessions on an existing product and share recordings or short summaries with the people who make decisions. Seeing a real user struggle is often more persuasive than any argument.
Moving from emerging to structured

This stage is about making UX less dependent on individuals. Define a basic design process, create a shared place for research findings, and start a simple pattern library. Make the case for dedicated roles by showing the work already done and the problems it caught early.
Moving from structured to integrated

The shift here is from service to partner. Push for designers and researchers to be involved at discovery, not just delivery. Connect UX work to outcomes that leadership tracks, like task completion, support volume or retention. Build relationships with product and engineering leads so UX has a seat when priorities are set.
Moving from integrated to user-driven

At this point the work is cultural. Make research easy for anyone to access and act on. Invite people from across the business to observe sessions. Help leaders build the habit of asking for user evidence. Measure and share the impact of user-centered decisions so the practice keeps earning trust.
Common traps along the way
Skipping stages.
Buying tools or hiring a large team doesn't create maturity if the organization isn't ready to use them.
Measuring activity instead of influence.
The number of research studies matters less than whether they change decisions.
Relying on one champion.
If progress depends on a single leader, it can stall when they leave.
Progress, not perfection

UX maturity isn't a badge you earn once. Organizations move up and sometimes slide back as teams, leaders and priorities change. Use the model as a mirror: understand where you stand today, pick the next realistic step, and focus there. Small, steady moves up the ladder do more than ambitious plans that never take root.

children.text: Centralize research for better decisions.

Most teams do more research than they realize. Interviews, usability tests, surveys, support reviews and sales calls all generate insight. The trouble is that it usually ends up scattered across slide decks, personal notes and old chat threads. Six months later, someone runs the same study again because nobody could find the first one.

A UX research repository fixes that. It's a single, searchable home for what your team has learned about users, organized so that anyone can find evidence when they need to make a decision. Done well, it turns research from a series of one-off projects into a growing body of knowledge.
What a research repository is (and isn't)
A repository isn't just a folder of reports. Reports are useful, but they're long, tied to a specific question, and hard to search for a single insight.

A good repository stores research at a more useful level of detail: the raw material, the individual observations and the insights drawn from them, all linked together. That lets someone ask "What do we know about how users handle invoices?" and get an answer that pulls from several studies at once.
Choose a simple structure
Start with a structure your team can understand at a glance. Most repositories are built around a few core building blocks:
Studies:
the research project itself, including the goal, method, date and participants.
Evidence:
raw material such as notes, recordings, transcripts and survey responses.
Observations:
specific things a participant said or did.
Insights:
patterns you've drawn from several observations, written as clear statements.
You can build this in a dedicated research tool, a database in your existing workspace or even a well-organized spreadsheet. The tool matters far less than the consistency of the structure.
Think in atomic insights

The idea of atomic research is to break findings into small, self-contained units that can be reused. Instead of one report with twenty findings buried inside, each insight becomes its own entry, linked to the evidence that supports it.
A strong atomic insight is:
Specific:
it describes one clear pattern or need.
Evidence-backed:
it links to the observations and studies behind it.
Plain:
anyone on the team can read it and understand it without context.
Living:
it can be strengthened, refined or retired as new research comes in.
Over time, insights that keep getting supported by new studies become your most reliable knowledge about users.
Tag consistently so things can be found
Tagging is what makes a research repository searchable. It's also where most repositories become messy.
Keep a controlled tag list rather than letting everyone invent their own. Useful tag groups often include:
Product area or feature
User type or segment
Journey stage, such as onboarding, daily use or renewal
Theme, such as trust, speed or collaboration
Assign one person to own the tag list, review it every few months, and merge duplicates. A smaller, cleaner set of tags beats a huge, inconsistent one every time.
Drive adoption from day one
The hardest part isn't building the repository. It's getting people to use it. A few habits help:
Make adding research part of finishing a study, not an optional extra.
Use templates so contributing takes minutes, not hours.
Link insights directly in product specs, design reviews and roadmap discussions.
Share a short digest of new insights regularly so people see the repository as useful, not just as storage.
When stakeholders see insights cited in real decisions, they start going to the repository on their own.
Maintain it like a product
A research repository needs care, just like anything else your team builds. Without it, outdated insights pile up and trust erodes.

Schedule light maintenance: archive old studies that no longer reflect the product, mark insights that may need fresh validation, and clean up tags. Be mindful of privacy too. Store consent records, remove personal details that aren't needed, and limit access to sensitive recordings.
Build knowledge that compounds

The real value of a repository shows up over time. Each new study adds to what you already know instead of starting from zero. New team members get up to speed faster. Debates get settled with evidence. And research stops disappearing the moment a project ends.

Start small with one structure, a short tag list and the studies you've run recently. Keep it tidy and keep it connected to decisions, and your repository will become one of the most valuable tools your team has.

children.text: Affordable UX research techniques for small teams.

There's a common belief that real UX research needs a lab, a recruiting agency and a specialist team. That belief keeps a lot of small teams guessing when they don't have to. Most of the value in research comes from talking to the right people and watching them use your product, and neither of those requires a big budget.
What it does require is focus. When money and time are tight, you need to be clear about what you're trying to learn and pick the cheapest method that can answer it. Here's how to do that.
Start with a sharp question

Lean research falls apart when the goal is vague. "Learn about our users" is too broad to act on. "Find out why trial users don't finish setting up their first project" is something you can answer in a week.
Write your question down, then list the decisions it will inform. If the answer won't change anything you're about to do, skip that study and pick one that will.
Guerrilla usability testing
Guerrilla testing means grabbing people quickly and informally to try your product or prototype. It's fast, cheap and surprisingly revealing.
Ask people in a coffee shop, a coworking space or a community event if they'll spare a few minutes.
Give them one or two realistic tasks and ask them to think aloud.
Watch where they hesitate, misread or backtrack.

The catch is that strangers may not match your real audience. Guerrilla tests work best for general usability issues like confusing labels, unclear navigation and hidden buttons, rather than deep questions about a specialist workflow.
Remote interviews with real users
Video calls have made interviews almost free. A short conversation with five or six real users will often surface the same handful of problems over and over, which tells you where to focus.
A few tips to get more from them:
Recruit from your own audience: existing customers, newsletter subscribers or people who've contacted support.
Offer a small thank-you, like a gift card or an extended trial, instead of paying professional rates.
Ask about past behavior ("Tell me about the last time you...") rather than hypotheticals ("Would you use...").
Record the call with permission so you can focus on listening.
Use the data you already have
You're probably sitting on research material already. Support tickets, sales call notes, app store reviews, chat transcripts and feedback forms are full of real language from real users.
Spend an afternoon reading through them and grouping recurring themes. You'll often find the same complaint phrased a dozen different ways. That's a strong signal, and it cost you nothing to collect.
Product analytics help too. Even basic tools can show where people drop off in a flow, which tells you where to aim your next round of testing.
Low-cost tools and quick studies
A few methods give you useful answers with very little setup:
Five-second tests:
Show a screen briefly, then ask what people remember. Great for checking whether a page communicates its purpose.
First-click tests:
Ask where someone would click to complete a task. If the first click is wrong, the rest of the journey usually goes badly.
Card sorting:
Ask users to group topics in a way that makes sense to them. Useful for navigation and information architecture.
Short surveys:
Keep them to a few focused questions and include one open-ended prompt.
Many of these can be run with free or low-cost tools, or simply with a shared slide deck and a video call.
Keep it lightweight but rigorous
Cheap doesn't have to mean sloppy. A few habits keep lean UX research trustworthy:
Write a simple plan: the question, who you'll talk to, and the tasks or prompts.
Avoid leading questions. "How easy was that?" nudges people toward "easy."
Take notes in a consistent format so patterns are easy to spot.
Share findings quickly, in plain language, with clear next steps.
And be honest about limitations. Five interviews won't tell you how common a problem is across your whole user base. They will tell you that the problem exists and roughly why.
Small budgets, real answers

The biggest risk for small teams isn't doing research badly. It's not doing it at all. A handful of conversations, a few scrappy tests and an afternoon with your support inbox can change the direction of a product.
Pick one question, choose the simplest method that answers it, and talk to real people this week. Good UX research is a habit, not a line item, and you can start building it with whatever you have.

children.text: The convenience of grocery delivery is undeniable. From the comfort of your home or office, on a computer, tablet, or phone, you can do your grocery shopping and have it delivered to your home. It's no wonder that
FMI.org
's Digital Shopper survey has predicted that by 2022 consumers could spend as much as $100 billion on online grocery shopping. I will be discussing one such product specifically.
This Milkbasket UX review looks at the app purely from a design and usability perspective.
About Milkbasket

Milkbasket, a Gurugram-based micro-delivery startup, operates in Bangalore, Gurugram, Dwarka (Delhi), Noida, Ghaziabad, Greater Noida and Hyderabad, allows users to order their daily supplies until midnight and delivers them in the early morning hours. It has also begun a subscription service system for users who need the same items delivered daily.

In its early years, Milkbasket only focused on milk delivery. Still, it has started exploring new categories to enter and might soon begin delivering prescribed medicine in some cities as well. Milk delivery is now a small portion of the startup's business.
Milkbasket, India’s first and largest micro-delivery platform has been recognized as ‘Startup of the Year’ 2017 at the 7th Small Business Awards.
Business

Milkbasked is a Small low-cost-high-margin grocery item (LCHMGI). Transaction amounts are comparatively lesser in volume. So the customers will be okay with a prepaid wallet. Also, they usually come with a good return policy from the supplier. LCHMGI — one can afford a simple no-questions-asked return policy(NQARP).
The software professional and entrepreneur in me has critically analysed its success mantra as follows:

It's a prepaid wallet App (like Uber) where anything added to the cart (up to the wallet value) is delivered until midnight in a day. The amount is deducted from the wallet. There is no cash payment required.
Milkbasket only delivers once a day (by 6 am)
Why?

It is night, it is late, and you just realised you still need to buy the milk, eggs and required bread for breakfast tomorrow. Hoping for the best, you try your neighbourhood Kirana store, but it is all closed. That is where you realise the need for the Milkbasket app that can help. Put everything you need into the shopping basket and head to bed. Whatever is in your basket will arrive at your doorstep between 5.00 am and 7.00 am the following day without having to check out or Key in your payment details.
Reach

With a daily reach of over 35,000 households and serving 10,000+ families every morning in Gurgaon, Milkbasket delivers the highest number of grocery orders in the NCR region. Its vision is to become the default mom & pop shop for over a million households in the next 3–5 years.

Having achieved positive unit economics within the first six months of the launch, Milkbasket is the most capital-efficient model in the online grocery space compared to its domestic and global peers.
Objectives of the review

It's essential to start your review by positioning your objectives. It sets the tone and ensures that you and your stakeholders have the exact expectations — whether you present your check or send it via email.
Some objectives or outcomes could include:
Identify opportunities
Substantiate design changes
Identify technical issues
Discuss UX improvements
But then, I am in no hurry to jump to conclusions,
The User

Busy. Online. Well off. Willing to put money in a prepaid wallet. I need more time (and mind) to remember things. Looking for convenience — Keep adding items to the cart as you place. No checkout is required. Won't mind if an extra element is ordered because it's an LCHMGI, and there's NQARP. Also, I Don't have time to sit around for deliveries. The most likely time to find them a home — is 6 am. What are people want for sure at 6? Milk — Milk availability is the most significant stress point for modern-day women.
Challenges
Milkbasket is a good app, so reviewing it will take work. I will be ignoring the operational side altogether. Let's go!
Overlapping Visual Hierarchy

Visual Hierarchy ranks design elements and influences in the order you want your users to view them. By applying principles like contrast, scale, balance and more, you can help establish each element in its rightful place and support the most critical factors stand out. However, the landing screen was messed up.

Being a designer, sometimes it is okay to go beyond your standard patterns. The scaling and sizing are creating chaos and not working; colour and contrast are disturbing — too much is happening — a lack of perspective. I will not go into details; however, one can read the Key Principles of Visual Hierarchy in UX Design.
Inconsistent Icon language
The icons are not following a standard design language. Icons are significant in the modern-day world because:

Icons exist to facilitate better, clearer and faster communication. The main aim of icons is to help users find, understand and execute actions efficiently. One can say icons were a manifestation of — a picture can say a thousand words.
Most designers rely on icons as an essential element of design. Designed well, they convey ideas more quickly than words and often take up less space.
Icons symbolise brands, products, ideas, and messages. Hence a design language is a must. For example:
However, this thing needs to be improved in this app. I can see three distinct icon languages, and none of them merges the communication from 3 different generations of design.
As a designer, for me, this is an eyesore.
Icons enhance your design, making it look brighter, neater and appealing to the eyes.
Creating brand recall and consistent brand language is easier if you have a distinct icon library.

Also, Micro-interactions are good. Identifying the places where animation has utility is only half the story. If you're going to use animations in your designs, you should build them well, and that is only possible when a spirit is a natural part of the design process. How Functional Animation Helps Improve User Experience
https://airbnb.design/
How many fonts are too many fonts?

Can you justify introducing another font into the mix for your communication? Probably not, but sometimes. While there aren't any definitive rules, it's best to keep that third font out of the picture and stick to two.

children.text: Although you can be excused for thinking that Hierarchy is about using different weights and sizes, it can be complicated. The crucial thing is the contrast.

Even when dealing with just a single font in a design, any minor adjustments to, for example, the line height of your paragraphs or the spacing in your headlines can dramatically change the balance of the whole thing.
Inconsistency in Grids

Implementation of most design projects involves collaboration between designers and developers. Nothing is worse for a UI designer than submitting a pixel-perfect design mockup and finding it looks completely different in production.

When designing a grid, consider the constraints on your design. For example, most of your users might be using a particular device (such as a phone). It means that all design decisions (including the grid) need to consider this constraint. Learning to design with limitations is a skill that will help you focus on what's important to your users.
Misplaced functionalities
I was in a different city during COVID restrictions. Luckily the 2nd city was also under the delivery service area. However, as a user, it was a nightmare to change the address. Here is why:

It was a nightmare; eventually, I had to use another app to order essentials. The best way to create something new is to look for references so that the first clients understand what it is about and can make associations.

What does it mean? It means that users spend most of their time on other websites (in case they do not know yours). It means they prefer similar sites to the ones they frequent and are already familiar with. That's why it's better not to be over-original or over-creative.

This norm was coined by Jakob Nielsen, director of the Nielsen Norman Group, which he co-founded with Apple's vice president of research. I do not know; I get the impression that he does know something about the topic :).
A practical case of this law would be any e-commerce.
https://lawsofux.com/jakobs-law
Complex/Bad Architecture
Continuing with the problem above, I spent hours trying to figure it out; ultimately, I located the solution, but at the least expected place.
I do not see the point that the Address change was shifted to another place. Here is my journey of an address change.
Further, why do two separate navigation exist? I also noticed referral program and payment etc., links.
I see some severe UX flaws here. I don't even know the need to discuss this any further.
Is communication missing?

Banner ads (static or dynamic) have their place in the mobile world, but with tiny screens, a much better option is to turn them into rich media. Tap-to-expand banners or mobile videos will give you more engagement.
Yeah! Stepping into new Whatever…
What is the app talking about here? A Wasted space is a wasted opportunity.
Further, one should be careful not to spend too much space on communication — eventually, every scroll counts.
Where is the cart?
There were individual pages. I realised the cart was not visible due to a background banner. We can avoid this.

Also, as I dived in deep, I realised category pages are not laid out well — different layouts, which we can easily avoid. I wonder why Layout 2 is not used for Layout 1. Design 2 is better and solves the purpose of Layout 1 too.
How much scrolling is too much scrolling?
I don't see a reason to have this long page; we have established UX practices in an app where categories are more or less the same — utilise a sticky footer or other means.
“Scrolling is a continuation. Clicking is a decision.”
Sticky Navigation is a Great Tool

Any site can benefit from sticky navigation. If you employ infinite scrolling, users will probably like having the ability to jump back to the top of the page with one tap rather than continuously swiping.
Scrolling fatigue has two results:
The first is called "zombie scrolling" and refers to the idea that a user slowly loses focus, tunes out their attention, and becomes less susceptible to your standard bait and hook or CTA.
The second result is "rage-quitting" or the "tl;dr" and occurs when a user becomes frustrated with scrolling and leaves a site without digesting its important points or getting any takeaway.
Further…

There are minor inconsistencies in the background colour palette — grinding in product placement ad glitches here and there. However, I am not providing any solution here. I am not getting paid after all. 😂
No, I am not associated with Milkbasket. I just wanted to review one of the most used apps in 2020.

children.text: Learn how UX and CX work together to create memorable customer experiences.

People often use the two terms as if they mean the same thing. They don't, and mixing them up leads to gaps no one owns. One team ships a clean, fast checkout. Another team answers support calls from people who were charged twice. Each team did its job, and the customer still had a bad day.
Getting UX vs CX right isn't about choosing a side. It's about knowing where each one starts and ends, and making sure the handoffs between them don't leak.
What UX and CX actually mean
User experience (UX)
is how it feels to use a specific product: an app, a website, a dashboard, a kiosk. Can you find what you need? Does the interface make sense? Can you finish the task without friction?
Customer experience (CX)

is the whole relationship someone has with a company. It covers the ad they saw, the sales call, the onboarding email, the product itself, the invoice, the support chat and the renewal notice. UX is one important part of that relationship, but only one part.
A simple way to hold it in your head:
UX asks, "Can people use this well?"
CX asks, "Do people want to keep doing business with us?"
Who owns each one
In most organizations, UX sits with product and design. Designers, researchers and product managers shape flows, run usability tests and decide what ships in the interface.

CX is usually spread wider. Marketing owns the first impression, sales owns the promise, operations owns delivery, support owns the rescue, and finance owns billing. Some companies have a dedicated CX lead or team, but even then, they rarely control every touchpoint directly.
That spread is exactly why problems slip through. When everyone owns a slice, nobody owns the seams between slices.
How each is measured
The two disciplines track different signals, and both sets matter.
UX metrics focus on the interaction itself:
Task success rate: did people complete what they came to do?
Time on task and error rate
Usability test findings and severity ratings
Ease-of-use scores gathered right after a task
CX metrics look at the relationship over time:
Customer satisfaction scores after key moments
Net Promoter Score and similar loyalty measures
Retention, churn and repeat purchase
Support ticket volume, reasons and resolution time

Here's the useful part: the numbers often explain each other. A rise in support tickets about "where is my order" might trace back to a confusing order status screen. A drop in task success on a settings page might show up weeks later as churn. If your UX and CX dashboards never sit side by side, you'll miss these connections.
Where the gaps usually show up
Silos tend to break the experience in predictable places:
Promises vs reality.
Marketing describes a feature one way, and the product works another way.
Handoffs between channels.
A customer starts in the app, gets stuck, calls support, and has to explain everything again.
Billing and account changes.
These flows are often owned by finance or engineering and get little design attention.
Edge cases.
Refunds, cancellations and failed payments are rare for the business but memorable for the customer.
None of these are pure UX problems or pure CX problems. They live in between.
How to break the silos
You don't need a reorganization to align UX and CX. You need shared visibility and a few shared habits.
Map the full journey together.
Bring design, support, marketing and operations into one session and map a real customer's path, start to finish. Mark who owns each step and where the handoffs are.
Share research both ways.
Let support teams sit in on usability tests. Let designers read support tickets and listen to calls. Each group sees problems the other can't.
Pick a few joint metrics.
Choose one or two journey-level outcomes, like successful first order or renewal rate, that both teams report on.
Fix the seams first.
When prioritizing, give extra weight to problems that cross team lines. They're the ones most likely to be ignored.
Use the same language for the customer.
Shared personas or journey stages help everyone describe the same person the same way.
Why the best products win at both

A great interface can't save a broken promise, and great service can't fully cover for a confusing product. When UX vs CX stops being a debate and becomes a partnership, the experience starts to feel consistent. People notice that consistency, even if they can't name it.
Closing thought

Start small. Pick one journey that matters, look at it end to end, and invite the people who own each piece into the same room. You'll likely find that the biggest improvements aren't on any single team's roadmap yet.

children.text: A beginner-friendly guide to APIs for product designers.

You don't need to write code to design great products. But if you never look past the screen, you'll keep running into the same surprises: the field that can't be edited, the list that loads in pieces, the error message nobody designed. Most of those surprises trace back to one thing you can learn in an afternoon: how APIs work.
This isn't about turning designers into engineers. It's about knowing enough to ask better questions earlier, so your designs survive contact with real data.
What an API actually is

An API (application programming interface) is a set of rules that lets one piece of software ask another for something. Your app's interface doesn't store the user's orders or calculate their shipping cost. It asks a server, and the server answers.

A useful mental model is a restaurant. The interface is the dining room. The kitchen is the backend. The API is the menu and the waiter: it defines what you can order, how to ask for it, and what comes back.
Most APIs you'll hear about follow a simple pattern:
A request
: "Give me this user's last ten orders."
A response
: a structured chunk of data, usually in a format called JSON, with fields like
order_id
status
and
total
A status
: a code that says whether it worked, failed, or needs something else first.
That's most of it. Everything else is detail.
Why APIs matter to your designs
When you understand APIs for designers' everyday work, a few things change in how you design.
Feasibility gets clearer.

If the API doesn't return a field, the interface can't show it without new backend work. A dashboard card showing "time since last login" might look trivial, but if that data isn't exposed, it's a project, not a tweak. Knowing this lets you have the conversation before the design is approved, not after.
Data states stop being an afterthought.

Every screen backed by an API has more than one state. Real data comes back empty, partial, very long, or in a shape you didn't expect. Designing only the happy path means engineers end up inventing the rest.
Latency becomes something you design for.

API calls take time, and that time varies. A search that feels instant on office Wi-Fi can lag on a train. Loading skeletons, optimistic updates and progress indicators are design decisions, and they depend on knowing which actions wait on the network.
Errors become part of the experience.
Requests fail. Servers time out, sessions expire, payments get declined. If you know the common failure cases, you can design helpful recovery paths instead of a generic "Something went wrong."
The states every API-backed screen needs
A practical checklist you can use on almost any screen:
Loading
: what the user sees while waiting.
Empty
: no data yet, and what to do about it.
Partial
: some data loaded, some still coming or missing.
Success
: the normal, populated view.
Error
: something failed, with a clear next step.
Edge content
: very long names, huge numbers, missing images.
If you design all six, you've already closed most of the gaps that cause rework.
Questions to ask your engineers
You don't need technical vocabulary to have a useful conversation. Try questions like these:
Which data on this screen comes from an API, and which is already in the app?
Is there one call for this screen, or several?
How long does this request usually take?
What happens if it fails? Can we retry automatically?
Are results paginated? How many items come back at once?
Can this field ever be empty or null?
Each answer shapes a design decision. Engineers usually appreciate being asked, because it means fewer surprises for them too.
How to learn the basics
Learning APIs for designers is mostly about exposure, not theory. You can build real understanding without a course or a coding bootcamp.
Look at real responses.
Open your browser's developer tools, go to the Network tab, and watch what loads when you use a web app. You'll see requests and the JSON they return.
Read API documentation.
Public APIs from well-known services often have readable docs with example responses. Skim a few to see how data is structured.
Try a request tool.
Free tools like Postman let you send requests and see responses without writing code.
Ask for a walkthrough.
Sit with an engineer for thirty minutes while they explain the APIs behind a feature you designed.
Design with real data.
Ask for sample responses and use them in your mockups instead of placeholder text.
Better collaboration, not a new job

Understanding APIs won't make you a backend developer, and it shouldn't. What it gives you is a shared language with the people who build your designs. You'll catch feasibility issues earlier, design states that would otherwise be forgotten, and spend less time in rework.
Start small. Pick one screen you're working on this week, find out which API calls power it, and design every state those calls can return. That habit alone will make your work noticeably stronger.

children.text: Simplicity creates faster, better user experiences.

When people hear "make it simpler," they often picture cutting features until there's barely anything left. That's not what simplicity means. Some of the most capable tools you use every day feel simple, not because they do less, but because they make what they do easy to understand and easy to get done.
Simplicity in UX design is about removing friction, not removing value. It's the difference between a product that makes you think about the product and one that lets you think about your task.
Simplicity is about friction, not feature count
Friction is anything that slows someone down or makes them hesitate: an unclear label, an extra step, a decision they didn't need to make, a screen packed with options that don't apply to them.

A product with fifty features can feel simple if the right ones show up at the right time. A product with five features can feel complicated if they're hard to find or confusingly named. So instead of asking "What can we remove?", ask "What's getting in the way?"
Why simplicity wins
Simple products tend to win for a few practical reasons:
People learn them faster,
so they reach value sooner
They make fewer mistakes,
which means less frustration and less support load
They feel faster,
even when the underlying system is the same
They're easier to grow,
because a clean foundation makes new features easier to fit in
They earn trust,
since clarity signals that the team knows what it's doing
Complexity, by contrast, piles up quietly. Every added option, setting, or exception feels small on its own. Together they create a product that only experts can navigate.
How to simplify a product
Simplifying is a discipline, not a one-time cleanup. These steps give you a practical starting point.
Get clear on the core job.
Write down the main thing people come to your product to do. Everything on a screen should either support that job or get out of the way.
Watch real people use it.
Friction is easiest to spot when you see someone pause, backtrack, or hunt for a button.
Cut steps, not capabilities.
Look for steps you can combine, skip, or automate. Can you prefill a field, remember a choice, or infer something instead of asking?
Use smart defaults.
Most people never change settings, so make the default the best option for most of them.
Reveal complexity gradually.
Show the essentials first and keep advanced options one click away. That way new users aren't overwhelmed and experts still get what they need.
Group and order with purpose.
Put related things together and the most common actions first.
Simplify the language too
Words are often the biggest source of hidden complexity. Internal jargon, clever labels, and long explanations all make people work harder.
A few rules help:
Use the words your users use, not your team's internal terms
Prefer short, specific labels over clever ones
Cut any sentence that doesn't help someone act or decide
Say one thing per message
If you need a paragraph to explain how a feature works, consider whether the feature itself could be clearer.
Visual simplicity supports clarity
A cluttered screen makes everything feel harder, even simple tasks. Visual simplicity isn't about minimalism as a style. It's about helping people see what matters.
Establish a clear hierarchy so the most important element stands out
Use whitespace to separate groups instead of extra lines and boxes
Limit the number of type sizes, colors, and button styles
Remove decoration that doesn't help understanding
The goal is a screen where people know where to look first, second, and third.
Watch out for false simplicity

Not every reduction makes things simpler. Hiding important options behind vague icons, removing labels to look clean, or cramming everything into a single menu can all make a product harder to use, even if it looks minimal.

Real simplicity in UX is measured by how easily people get things done, not by how empty the screen looks. If people struggle to find something they need, you've moved the complexity rather than removed it.
Make simplicity a habit
Products naturally get more complex over time as new requests come in. To keep things simple, make it part of how you work:
Ask what each new feature replaces or improves, not just what it adds
Review older parts of the product for features nobody uses
Treat confusion in support requests as a design problem to fix

Simplicity wins because it respects people's time and attention. Focus on the core job, remove friction wherever you find it, and reveal depth only when it's needed. Do that consistently, and your product will feel lighter and faster, even as it grows more capable.

children.text: Clear writing improves usability.

Every product has a voice, whether you planned one or not. It speaks through button labels, error messages, empty screens, and confirmation notes. These small bits of text, often called microcopy, guide people through your product more than most visuals do.

Good UX copy is easy to overlook because it just works. Bad copy shows up immediately as confusion, hesitation, and support requests. Here are practical UX writing tips you can apply to the words in your product today.
Start with clarity over cleverness
The first job of any interface text is to be understood. Clever wordplay and brand jokes can be fun, but they often slow people down or get lost on anyone who isn't paying full attention.
A few habits help:
Use plain, everyday words your users already know
Put the most important information first
Keep sentences short and focused on one idea
Cut filler words like "simply," "just," and "please note that"
If someone has to read a line twice to understand it, rewrite it.
Write buttons that say what happens
Buttons are some of the most important words in your product. People should know exactly what will happen before they tap.
Rules for better buttons:
Use specific verbs.
"Save draft," "Send invoice," and "Create project" beat "Submit," "OK," or "Continue."
Match the button to the heading.
If the dialog asks "Delete this file?", the button should say "Delete file," not "Yes."
Keep them short.
Two or three words is usually enough.
Make destructive actions obvious.
Clear wording, combined with visual cues, helps prevent costly mistakes.
Stay consistent.
If it's "Remove" in one place, don't call it "Delete" somewhere else for the same action.
A good test: if you read only the buttons on a screen, can you still tell what the screen is for?
Make error messages helpful
Errors are where UX copy matters most, because people are already frustrated. A good error message explains what went wrong and how to fix it, without blame.
Strong error messages:
Say what happened
in plain language, not codes or technical jargon
Explain how to fix it,
such as "Enter a date in the future"
Appear next to the problem,
not only at the top of the page
Avoid blaming the user,
so "That password doesn't match" works better than "You entered the wrong password"
Keep a calm tone,
without exclamation marks or jokes
Compare "Invalid input" with "Phone numbers need 10 digits." The second one tells people exactly what to do next.
Turn empty states into guidance
An empty state is what people see when there's nothing to show yet: no projects, no messages, no results. Too often these screens are left blank or say only "No data."
Use empty states to help people move forward:
Explain what will appear here once there's content
Offer a clear next action, like "Create your first project"
For empty search results, suggest what to try instead
Empty states are especially important for new users, since they see them more than anyone else.
Find the right tone for the moment
Your product can have a consistent voice while adjusting its tone to the situation. Voice is your personality. Tone is how that personality responds to the moment.
Celebration moments,
like finishing a setup, can be warm and a little upbeat
Routine tasks
should be neutral and efficient
Errors and problems
call for calm, clear, and reassuring language
Sensitive topics,
such as payments, health, or account deletion, need extra care and plain honesty
Ask yourself how the person is likely feeling at that moment, and write for that.
Keep it consistent
Consistency makes a product feel trustworthy and easier to learn. Decide on a few basics and stick to them:
Sentence case or title case for headings and buttons
How you refer to the user and to your product
Preferred terms for key actions and objects
Rules for numbers, dates, and punctuation
A short content style guide, even a single page, keeps everyone writing the same way.
Test it, then keep going

You can test UX copy just like any other part of the design. Read it aloud. Show it to someone unfamiliar with the product and ask what they'd expect to happen. Look at support tickets for repeated questions, because they often point to unclear wording.

Writing better UX copy isn't about being a great writer. It's about being clear, specific, and kind at every point where people need guidance. Fix your buttons, errors, and empty states first, set a consistent tone, and you'll see how much smoother your product feels.
